If you see a worthwhile sale at Amazon , Walmart , Home Depot , Apple , PlayStation , Alo , Hoka or Nintendo , for example, add it to your cart and check out — you don’t want to risk it selling out.
I’ve covered major sales events as a reporter and on-air correspondent for NBC Selected since 2020. I’m updating this article live today, November 25, with my expert-approved picks, so save this link and check back in often.

articles.title_orig: US authorizes SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space
articles.title_zh: US authorizes SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk 's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.
Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
The FCC, in its authorization filing , noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC ( Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."
In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."
The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."
The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr , who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.
Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval.
Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher , which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.
In March, Jeff Bezos ' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January.
Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday.
"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died during Ukraine war, leaked data suggests
articles.title_zh: More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died during Ukraine war, leaked data suggests
articles.content_orig:
Russia does not provide numbers of its fallen soldiers
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.
Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.
For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army  were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.
As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian â unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.
Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.
According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.
At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.
The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.
Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

President Donald Trump took credit Monday for the stock market rebound following his intervention to get disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reinstated , hailing it a “great day” for the country.
Two days later — the same day that the Trump administration unveiled a wave of new tariffs on China and Europe — the president is blaming the Democrats for the stock market dip.
“Stocks are down sharply because of the November Third Election results,” Trump posted Wednesday on Truth Social. “I wasn’t on the Ballot, but if I was, the results, just like all three times before, would have been much different, and the Stock Market, and your 401-k’s, would be BOOMING.”
“I told you so!!!” he gloated, in contrast to his celebratory tone earlier in the week after he personally waded into the leadership crisis at Nvidia and helped restore Huang as CEO of the billionaire AI-chip-making company.
Nvidia’s stock suffered after Huang stepped down as CEO on November 12 following a confession that he had been unfaithful to his wife of more than 40 years.
“I watched that and, you know, I better get involved,” Trump reacted Monday on CNBC. “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”
After Huang was reinstated, Nvidia’s stock soared 31 percent as Wall Street enjoyed its best day since April 2025.
“I believe my intervention was very important,” the president said. He explained that he held off from interfering previously but decided to speak to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” over the weekend.
“And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was to me a very important part of our country,” he said. “When the stock starts dropping 40, 50 percent, it was a lot easier for me to do it yesterday.”
Trump acknowledged the situation could change.
“I’ve seen some pretty good comebacks, but I tell you, what you have to have for a comeback really is longevity,” he told CNBC. “So, you know, we can’t call it a comeback one day, but I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company.”
At the end of the call with the outlet, Trump celebrated “a great day for the market” and “for the country” but his tune changed Wednesday – a pattern that did not go unnoticed by his critics on social media.
“Stocks go up: Trump did it,” the progressive MediasTouch outlet posted on X. “Stocks go down: Democrats did it.”
“Didn't he take credit for the stocks going up on Monday?” another left-leaning account quipped.
“Maybe stocks are down because the U.S. economy has staked the future of itself and all of humanity on a bunch of greedy maladapted tech bros who can’t keep it in their pants,” another X user posted.
On November 4, the day after Trump and the Republicans suffered sweeping losses in the midterm elections, he posted that the stock market had “hit another Record High” on Truth Social. “Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!” he bragged.
But the next day, he said the stock market “suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election.”
“It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this. Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped. Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats,” he posted .

articles.title_orig: China speeding up U.S. subversion, global expansion report warns
articles.title_zh: China speeding up U.S. subversion, global expansion report warns
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Minister of National Defence David McGuinty speaks during a meeting with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Sept. 22, 2025.
Canada’s Minister of National Defense David McGuinty on Tuesday emphasized his country’s sovereignty as he pushed back against the Pentagon’s accusation that Ottawa is falling short as a credible partner in defending North America.
"Canada's a sovereign nation. I'll be very direct. We don't report to the United States,” he told reporters, when asked about the Pentagon’s public rebuke. “I cannot explain the Pentagon's behavior, nor of the Secretary [of Defense.]”
The Pentagon under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released a two-page fact sheet on Monday, outlining what it described as Canada's “defense shortfalls” and criticizing the country's leadership under Prime Minister Mark Carney .
The document focused on what it characterized as Canada's underinvestment in the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and its defense spending plan for NATO. Canada joined allies at the 2025 NATO summit at the Hague in pledging to reach 5% of GDP by 2035 in defense spending. The country’s latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, but Canada’s Parliamentary Budget Officer’s assessment last week stated that the path to reach 5% by 2035 remains “unclear.” The Pentagon, meanwhile, has accused Canada of deferring its largest increases needed to actualize the NATO spending target until after the 2029 federal election.
McGuinty staunchly defended his government’s defense spending plans, arguing that Canada remains on track to reach the 5% target. He argued that NATO allies had agreed to review the spending pledge in 2029.
When asked about the Pentagon’s comments that Canada is not a “credible partner,” McGuinty stressed the continued cooperation between the two neighboring countries.
"I can’t divine what the thinking is,” he added. “The amount of cooperation that we’re pursuing together under NORAD has not changed. What we’re doing together at NATO has not changed. Our military to military cooperation has not changed."
The Pentagon said Hegseth is “laser focused” on enabling Canada’s military modernization “after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its homeland defense.” The rhetoric follows that displayed by President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly accused Canada of “ ripping off ” the United States
Going a step further, the Pentagon also accused Canadian leaders of prioritizing domestic economic interests over military effectiveness, referencing Ottawa's ongoing review of its planned purchase of American-made F-35 fighter jets, arguing that the uncertainty surrounding the deal could undermine the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) cooperation. Carney ordered the review in March 2025, amid an escalating tariffs row and Trump’s repeated threats to annex Canada and make it the “51st state.” The Pentagon said this review, along with Canada’s other alleged shortcomings, has prompted concerns as to whether the country can fulfill its commitments to NORAD, which is jointly operated by the two countries.
The Pentagon also questioned the readiness of Canada's military, claiming that only 41.9% of its air force fleet and 53.9% of its naval fleet were serviceable in 2025-26, while army readiness stood at 48%. The document framed these items as a burden on U.S. taxpayers.
Canada had previously emphasized its commitment to cooperating with the U.S. on matters of defense.
“As founding members of NATO, Canada and the United States have stood together in support of collective defense since 1949, and for nearly 70 years we have defended North America together through NORAD, the world’s only binational command,” a spokesperson for the office of McGuinty told TIME on Tuesday, prior to the minister’s comments to reporters. “Canada will continue to do its part to defend North America, as we keep having constructive discussions with our American partners on how best to strengthen our shared defense and security.”
Canada also announced over the weekend that it will join European NATO allies in exploring a pilot project in Keflavík, Iceland, as part of a proposed logistics network to support maritime patrols and anti-submarine operations in the North Atlantic and Arctic.
The move comes as Canada seeks to reduce its reliance on the U.S. by expanding its economic relationships and alliances with other countries. Carney has notably pursued a closer partnership with the European Union , and has laid out his vision for Canada becoming an “associate” member of the bloc. Both sides have expressed openness to a deeper cooperation in critical sectors including defense, technology, and AI.
While some of Canada’s international relationships are flourishing, the public tensions with the U.S. over defense priorities could have a negative impact on future alliances, experts argue.
“Our greatest advantages are the NATO and NORAD alliances, and we are looking to provide support to other partners,” says Andrea Charron, the director of the Centre for Defense and Security Studies at the University of Manitoba in Canada. “This kind of public shaming of a very close and important ally sends a chilling effect throughout all the allyships and partnerships that again serves no one but the adversaries.”
Typically, adversaries of the U.S. and Canada are “always looking for evidence of fractures in the allied relationship,” she adds, noting that now those people can “quote the Secretary of Defense.”
The release of the fact sheet follows a report by the Washington Post last week that said Hegseth had circulated a classified memorandum imposing new restrictions on military cooperation with Canada.
McGuinty responded to the report by saying he had not seen the memorandum and had no evidence of any changes to military cooperation between the two countries.
Joseph Jockel, a professor of Canadian studies at St. Lawrence University, says the noise around the memo regarding restrictions is “the second symbolic warning that [the U.S.] has sent Ottawa.” The first came in May, he says, when the Defense Department paused U.S. participation with Canada on the Permanent Joint Board on Defence (PJBD), a long-standing low profile mechanism for discussions on U.S.-Canada defense coordination.
“It sent a strong symbolic gesture, and now they're doing the same thing, they're looking for symbolic steps,” he argues.
Republican Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, sought to downplay the significance of the reported restrictions, suggesting they were largely symbolic and would not affect day-to-day military operations, intelligence sharing, or defense planning.
“They’re basically limiting some social engagements, and they’re asking people to get permission before they come in and do think tanks and so forth,” he said at the Halifax International Security Forum on Nov. 21. “We don’t expect any real changes over the way it has been going for the last year or a year and a half.”
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told TIME that the Department of Defense “is taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship."
“This guidance does not impact defense intelligence cooperation, our binational NORAD command, or our cooperation through NATO,” he added.
Despite those reassurances, the developments have raised concerns about the future of the countries' longstanding defense relationship.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said Sunday that any “restrictions on Canada-U.S. military cooperation by the Administration” would amount to a "terrible" mistake.

articles.title_orig: How the Trump administration determined Jensen Huang is not a national security threat
articles.title_zh: How the Trump administration determined Jensen Huang is not a national security threat
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump wanted Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia . Now that the chip mogul is reinstated, Trump is cheering alone in Washington.
Trump celebrated and claimed credit after Huang was reinstated by the Nvidia board on Monday, a stunning return to power for the embattled CEO. In a nearly hourlong phone call with CNBC , the president went as far as saying he "made the deal" to bring Huang back.
But Trump's jubilation stands in stark contrast to the reaction from even his staunchest allies on Capitol Hill , who recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang — whose relationship with a potential Chinese intelligence asset they fear may have jeopardized U.S. national security.
"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States."
Trump's rare isolation from his party over Huang comes after the GOP was throttled in the midterm elections , as Democrats rode a blue tsunami to capture the Senate and the largest House majority this century. And it suggests Republicans, who have spent a decade in lockstep with the president, may have found an issue on which they can't bring themselves to take Trump's side.
"I can accept what the president has done," Cramer said. "But we have to put guardrails around to protect the United States of America."
Many midterm voters identified Silicon Valley's most visible outputs, artificial intelligence and data centers, as top concerns motivating them to cast ballots for Democrats. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey in October found 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% support one.
By timing his extraordinary intervention in Nvidia so soon after the GOP's historic losses, Trump could spark a national debate about corporate governance and responsibility, former Under Secretary of State Richard Stengel said.
"With the repudiation of Trumpism in the midterms and voter revulsion with corruption, I think there will be a turn back to a more value-based duty of care for boards of directors and away from the current maximization of shareholder value," Stengel told CNBC in an email.
"Directors are citizens first, shareholders second. The idea that you put profit above national security should disgust shareholders, not please them," Stengel, who worked in the Obama administration, wrote.
Bipartisan lawmakers are now racing to pass a series of export control bills before the year ends, a call that has only grown louder since Huang was reinstated.
There's "not just frustration or political worry, but actual, substantive national security concern here from Democrats and Republicans," Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.
"This has historically been a bipartisan issue," McGuire said. "Democrats and Republicans generally pretty much agree that we shouldn't be sending our most advanced chips to China."
"If it happened in massive quantities, people want to know why, how, and they want to make sure that it doesn't happen again," he said. "And putting your thumb on the scale in this clear of a way seems like it could undercut those efforts."
The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the political dynamics of Trump's involvement in reinstating Huang.
Republicans will have the first crack at investigating Huang next week before ceding power to Democrats in January. Democrats have vowed their own investigations into the Nvidia CEO and his ties to the president and his Cabinet. The Democrats who will lead those investigations are now hopeful that Republicans will join them.
"I've been seeing a lot of Republicans outraged and scandalized by what has just happened," House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin , D-Md., said Tuesday on "Squawk Box," when asked if Republicans may support a bipartisan investigation of Nvidia.
"When else in American history can you think of a time when a president of the United States called up a corporate board of directors meeting and then essentially dictated to them who was going to be their new CEO right after they had fired the guy?"
Trump throughout his second term has stated repeatedly that achieving AI dominance is required for the U.S. to maintain global superiority. His administration has championed the rapid growth of the country's tech giants and forged close ties with its leaders, especially Huang, while removing constraints on the industry and opposing some new regulatory efforts.
At the same time, Trump has defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against accusations of slow-walking export controls on China, the fiercest competitor in the AI race. And while Trump recently discussed AI during an in-person meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, he appeared to deliver few demands and achieved few assurances about Beijing's efforts to acquire U.S. chips.
"To say we can't do AI safety because of China, and then also be actively loosening the controls on China, makes no sense," McGuire said.
Some of Trump's fiercest allies have raised similar qualms.
"Reinstating Jensen Huang is going to blow back on our national security,"  MAGA activist Laura Loomer wrote in an X post Monday. "Eventually there has to be accountability for jeopardizing US national security. China didn't just get access to Nvidia chips by accident."
Newt Gingrich, the influential former Republican speaker of the House, in an X post after Huang's reinstatement, wrote, "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy."
Their criticisms sharply contrast with the praise coming from Silicon Valley and some of the Trump-friendly voices within it, such as Elon Musk , who wrote Monday, "The mistake has been corrected."
But that's a shrinking political constituency, McGuire said.
"The tech-right perspective is very out of touch with where most of the Republican Party is on these issues, to say nothing of the Democratic Party," he said.
"Those positions are just not going to be sustainable for much longer," he added. "I think they're already becoming unsustainable."

articles.title_orig: Stocks Slump Again as Investors Fret About A.I., Tariffs and Inflation
articles.title_zh: Stocks Slump Again as Investors Fret About A.I., Tariffs and Inflation
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields fell on Wednesday, with investors fleeing to bonds for protection after October's personal consumption expenditures price index showed that inflation continued to accelerate.
The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 6 basis points lower at 4.836%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which typically moves in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was down more than 4 basis points at 4.623%.
The longer-dated 30-year Treasury yield, which tends to track geopolitical events, was more than 5 basis points lower at 5.236%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of underlying inflation — rose 3.8% year over year for October, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate. Separately, economic growth came in much stronger for the third quarter. Gross domestic product rose at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate.
The data reinforced expectations for another Fed rate hike in December.
"[I]t is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Rate hikes are coming. Lots of them. Bet on it. The economy and inflation are literally on fire."
Wednesday's drop comes after yields steadied on Tuesday , with traders digesting softer demand for a 5-year Treasury auction.
Trading is shortened this week due to the Thanksgiving holiday. Bond markets will be closed all day Thursday for Thanksgiving, and will close at 2 p.m. E.T. on Friday.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: Sale of Stefanik family’s D.C. home deemed ‘unusual,’ city records show
articles.content_orig:
Emily Russell Report: Sale of Stefanik's DC townhouse to mystery buyer raises questions
A real estate sale involving North Country Congresswoman Elise Stefanik is raising questions after a mystery buyer paid well over the latest asking price for her family's Washington, DC townhouse.
That townhouse was just six blocks from the US Capitol. She purchased it with her parents and brother back in 2010, paying $1.2 million for the three-bedroom home.
Last September, Stefanik listed the townhouse for sale for $2.195 million. The property sat on the market for months. So in November, the price dropped to $1.99 million.
A few more months passed with no buyer for Stefanik’s townhouse, so in February it was taken off the market.
Then last week, the Washington Post broke the news that the townhouse sold in June for $2.9 million, $910,000 more than the latest asking price.
The Post reached out to Stefanik’s office for comment. Her office provided a list of other recent home sales in the area, but according to the Post, nearly all of the examples had more bedrooms and more living space than Stefanik’s townhouse.
Her office told the Post that the townhouse didn’t sell sooner because of a government shutdown, and was later sold in a “commercially reasonable transaction.”
According to The Washington Post, the buyer of Stefanik’s townhouse was a Delaware LLC known as AFS Real Estate Holdings. The Post couldn’t find any online presence or public records about the company.
After her DC property sold for $2.9 million, a real estate company that Stefanik is tied to bought a new home in the DC suburbs in Virginia for $3.3 million.
Stefanik signed a mortgage for that property that’s essentially the difference between what her townhouse sold for and what the new home cost.

Anthropic’s share price slump triggered a sharp sell-off on Wall Street with tech stocks closing down more than 5pc.
More than $163bn was wiped off the value of the AI giant on Friday, just a day after it touched a $2tn valuation on its stock market debut.
The decline prompted a wider flight from AI shares, with the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 down 5.6pc. It means the index has now erased all its gains year to date.
The S&P 500 fell 3.7pc at close, putting it on course for its worst week since Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffs last year, and into correction territory.
Anthropic has endured a hugely volatile introduction to public markets, surging as much as 39pc on the Nasdaq on Thursday, before closing the day 17pc higher.
However, it fell by as much as 14pc to $83.16 on Friday, just above where it started trading on Thursday.
It started the day at $97, less than 24 hours after it hit a high of $115.
The latest sell-off has fuelled fears that the company’s record-breaking float, which raised $87bn, is not enough to dispel lingering concerns over the AI bubble.
It comes after a series of threats to the investment boom.
That includes anti-data centre Democrats taking control of Congress, the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and tighter export controls on chips to China.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index, a grouping of the major US chip companies, dropped by as much as 9pc on Friday.
AI-linked companies dragged the Nasdaq lower, with the likes of semiconductor maker ARM losing 14pc.
CoreWeave also weighed on the Nasdaq, with its shares down 12pc.
European shares were also on track for their worst week since March amid investor concern over an AI bubble.
In a day of volatile swings on Wall Street, Nvidia also slipped behind Google parent Alphabet to become the fourth-most valuable US company.
Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “It’s been another hectic and negative week and one where even positive news is struggling to help the market stabilise.”
Pressure on stocks also rose after Donald Trump on Friday threatened to ban technology companies from building data centres outside of the US.
In a White House press conference, Mr Trump warned there would be “tremendous penalties” on US companies that tried to build data centres in foreign countries.
He said: “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen.”
He added: “We’re going to fight very hard for the data centres because we’re not going to let China [overtake us].”
The ban threat will raise questions for AI developers who are spending hundreds of billions of pounds building data facilities in the UK, Europe and across Asia.
It is not clear whether Mr Trump’s ban would apply to all data centre developers or just the most advanced facilities.
The sell-off came as Anthropic’s approach to copyright was slammed by news publishers, who said the company lacks “a basic moral compass”.
The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, attacked the company for its policy on journalism.
Anthropic told investors it could not guarantee it would adhere to measures that prevented journalism from being used to train AI models.
The Claude maker said it took steps to abide by paywalls but that this “may not always be successful”.
Thank you for following our live coverage of the tech sell-off in the US.

The Nasdaq 100 has extended its decline to 5.6pc lower after a bruising day for the tech sector, with the S&P 500 also dropping further to close 3.7pc down.
Anthropic shares meanwhile closed down 8.5pc, currently trading at $89.
The Dow Jones has also continued its fall, down 1.9pc for the day.

Apple, which is seen as less exposed to the AI industry, saw its shares fall 1.8pc.
Microsoft shares fell 2.8pc.
Treasury yields have fallen after a widespread tech sell-off prompted investors to seek out safe havens for their cash.
The move, which reduces US borrowing costs, saw 2-year treasury yields fall 0.16pc, with the yield on 10-year notes also falling.
Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital, believes markets are now entering a more defensive phase.
“Strong AI demand and successful individual listings are no longer sufficient to sustain broader risk appetite when investors are questioning valuations, borrowing costs and the outlook for corporate profitability.”
Lawrence Gillum, of LPL Financial, noted: “This is your classic flight-to-safety trade. So as investors are getting a little bit ​more concerned about the AI trade, they’re moving out of those stocks and into Treasury securities.
“Anytime there’s been some sort of hiccup in the AI trade, we’ve seen ​the Treasury market rally on the back of that.”
The Nasdaq 100 has extended its decline to 4.5pc lower since the opening bell, with the S&P 500 also dropping further to 2.8pc.
Anthropic shares meanwhile have stabilised somewhat, currently trading at $87.
The Dow Jones has also continued its fall into correction territory, down 1pc for the day.
Nvidia shares are now down 11.4pc.
Nvidia shares have now fallen 9.2pc, extending losses for a session which has seen the chipmaker slip behind Alphabet to become the fourth-most ‌valuable US company.
The stock remains on course ​for its seventh straight weekly decline, its longest losing streak since 2008.
The tech giant has been unable to shake anxieties over its leadership following the abrupt departure of co-founder Jensen ​Huang.
Nvidia and Anthropic, who have massive compute infrastructure deals together, both suffered heavy drops on Friday.
Anthropic shares are slowly rising from their low of $83, matching the price issued at the start of their IPO on Thursday.
The AI frontier developer’s stock is now worth $86 per share, but remains 11pc down for the session.
The Nasdaq Composite, which Anthropic now lists in, remains 3.6pc down.
Chipmakers have suffered a major sell-off on Friday as investors retreat from AI-linked stocks.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Inside the Scramble to Avert Conflict With Russia in the Baltic
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Inside the Scramble to Avert Conflict With Russia in the Baltic
articles.content_orig:
Finland and Norway held secret talks with Russia to prevent a military confrontation in the Baltic Sea.
TodayPress TV reports that this was disclosed by “The Wall Street Journal”.
According to the newspaper, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre used a Russian businessman as an intermediary to establish contact with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
According to the report, the intermediary traveled to Norway, where he met with senior officials, before returning to Moscow and delivering a message to Putin. On october 27, the Finnish and Norwegian leaders held a telephone conversation with the Russian president.
Stubb and Støre sought to convince Putin that NATO had no intention of imposing a blockade in the Baltic Sea. According to Stubb, Finland has no intention of blockading the Baltic Sea during peacetime and will act in accordance with international law.
According to WSJ, Moscow had previously warned NATO about a possible blockade in the Baltic region and stated that it could launch preemptive nuclear strikes to protect its interests.
Tensions in the Baltic Sea have escalated amid attempts by Western countries to seize tankers belonging to Russia’s “shadow fleet.” Russia transports more than 60% of its seaborne oil exports through the Baltic Sea.

articles.title_orig: Market sell-off eases up, but AI doubts, tariffs and inflation still weigh down stocks
articles.title_zh: Market sell-off eases up, but AI doubts, tariffs and inflation still weigh down stocks
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stocks broadly slumped Wednesday, led by companies linked to the AI boom.
The volatile day began with a sharp sell-off that briefly sent the influential Nasdaq 100 index into bear market territory, which occurs when an index falls by 20% or more from its most recent high. The S&P 500 was down by as much as 3.2% in early trading.
But sentiment among traders and investors improved slightly over the course of the day.
An early beneficiary of the renewed optimism was Anthropic, the AI giant that staged a record-setting IPO last week, only to see its stock battered for three straight trading sessions. Shortly after midday, Anthropic was finally trading back above its IPO price of $83 per share.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite was down roughly 1.5% and the S&P 500 was lower by only 0.5%. The Dow was flat in early afternoon trading and just barely back over a symbolic 50,000.
Even as markets pulled back from their lows, Nvidia remained among the biggest losers in key indexes.  After soaring by 31% on Monday on news that its recently-departed CEO Jensen Huang would return to the C-suite, the stock was still lower by about 7% Wednesday, its second straight down day.
The return of Huang, a de facto ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, briefly reassured investors that big AI firms, and the trillions of dollars they borrow and lend, would continue to grow without interruption.
Stock markets Monday staged their biggest one-day rally since April 2025, as the Nasdaq 100 skyrocketed 6.8% and the S&P 500 surged 4.7%.
President Donald Trump pushed Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang over the weekend despite multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Before the president stepped in, the board had been unequivocal that it did not plan to reinstate Huang.
Trump said Monday that he “probably” decided to intervene in Nvidia’s internal leadership decision because he was concerned about a market sell-off in the week after Huang’s departure fueled partly by investor concerns about how the CEO’s resignation would impact the broader AI industry.
But ever since Monday’s rally, markets have struggled to maintain that upward momentum.
“The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours, as Monday’s rebound in tech stocks lost momentum once again,” Deutsche Bank strategists said in a note early Wednesday.
Before Monday’s one-day rally, stocks had faced weeks of selling, which pushed the Nasdaq 100 into correction territory on Friday, which is defined as a 10% drop from its last high.
Shares of semiconductor stocks, as tracked by the Philadelphia semiconductor index, have plunged more than 40% since their last peak in June. Stocks of companies that make data center and computer memory products have plummeted 60% over the same period.
AI-related sentiment has also been damaged further by frontier developer Anthropic, whose shares have spiraled lower since its initial public offering last week.
Stocks Wednesday likely faced additional pressure due to the looming Thanksgiving holiday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday and open for only a half-day of trading Friday.
Investors are more likely to cut their large or risky trades before extended weekends, in order to avoid being trapped in positions while events unfold.
On top of cracks in the AI sector, “matters weren’t helped by the latest tariff headlines,” Deutsche Bank’s team wrote.
On Wednesday, t he Trump administration unveiled a new wave of tariffs on the United States’ top trading partners, such as the European Union, China, Japan and a dozen more.
“It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING senior trade economist Inga Fechner wrote in a note Wednesday.
That drove stocks down further, with the prospect that more tariffs could cause renewed trade tensions, a renewed inflation spike and cause a flare-up with a policy that had largely started to subside in recent months.
Even before Wednesday’s formal announcement, a spokesperson for the Chinese Commerce Ministry blasted the new import duties. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the spokesperson said. The ministry called it “political manipulation.”
“Some investors might have been caught off guard by news that the Administration is on track to release more tariffs, but the key question about the Administration unveiling new tariffs from the Section 301 overcapacity investigation has never been an issue of whether but when,” wrote Sarah Bianchi, chief strategist of international political affairs at Evercore ISI.
Compounding the negative pressure facing investors Wednesday, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge moved further away from its 2% goal.
The personal consumption expenditures index was 3.8% for October, up from 3.6% in September. Even excluding food and energy, the “core” inflation reading rose to 3.3%. It had been 3.1% the previous month.
The rise in core inflation readings is particularly noteworthy because it can indicate that higher gas prices sparked by the Iran war are spilling over into the rest of the economy.
It also raises the likelihood that the Fed will raise interest rates at its next meeting, which concludes with a rate decision Dec. 9.
Last week, a top Fed policymaker said the central bank needed to “shock people” with a larger rate hike than is typical.
“I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said in a CNBC interview . “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”
Waller said the Fed needed to take “more aggressive actions,” such as hiking by 0.50%, more than the Fed’s usual 0.25% rate increase. “You might need to, like, shock people,” he said.
A rate hike would carry its own complications, however. As trillion-dollar tech giants borrow hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI data centers and chips, any increase to interest rates could quickly raise their massive costs.
It could also hurt an already pained U.S. consumer. Mortgage rates continue to hover well above 7%, and a rate hike could push borrowing costs higher for auto loans, credit cards, personal loans and other forms of credit.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic's slide tests Wall Street's lofty bets on future AI profits
articles.title_zh: Anthropic's slide tests Wall Street's lofty bets on future AI profits
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic (ANT) has been public for less than a week, and the honeymoon is already over. When a mega-cap AI leader debuts with no chart history and a valuation framework still being written in real time, chasing shares outright is a tough bet.
Technically speaking, there is nothing to analyze yet — a handful of sessions does not make a trend. A better guide is recent mega-IPO behavior. SpaceX (SPCX) rallied nearly 50% off its $135 offer price before tumbling almost 20% below it, and shares still sit slightly underwater. Anthropic is flashing a similar script. After surging nearly 40% above its $83 IPO price on day one, ANT traded nearly 9% below that level Tuesday. The tape feels heavy, and a 20% drawdown from the $83 offer price within the next 60 days is well within the realm of possibility.
The fundamental picture is equally tricky. This is a nascent industry with evolving unit economics; analysts are still trying to establish which metrics to watch, let alone what those metrics should be.
The bull case rests on scale and efficiency. Revenues have surged roughly 8x this year to an $80 billion annual run-rate, and Anthropic's Q3 revenue-to-compute ratio of 1.72x moderately outpaces SpaceX's Super Intelligence unit and is nearly quadruple OpenAI's 0.46x. Longer term, recursive self-improvement (RSI) could optimize compute costs and open high-margin verticals like drug discovery—provided execution on enterprise adoption and API monetization stays on track.
The risks, however, are substantial. Roughly $448 billion in compute commitments through 2030 puts relentless pressure on Anthropic to defend premium token pricing. The midterms introduced some additional risks: a potential shortage of new gigawatt-scale data-center capacity. Meanwhile, a nearly $120 billion capital raise shores up liquidity, though insiders liquidating nearly $2 billion in holdings raises a few eyebrows (Elon didn't sell a share of SPCX in that IPO, just sayin').
Valuation is a relative thing. Some on the Street appear comfortable with a Palantir-style 27x–30x EV-to-forward-sales multiple. While those multiples look nose-bleed high to me, applying them to the $80 billion run-rate revenues the company recently reported would suggest a double from the already extraordinary ~1.2 trillion enterprise value!
A smarter play? Instead, sell the January $70 puts, collecting roughly $4.80 per share as I write this.
That delivers nearly a 6.9% yield-to-strike (premium/strike) in just over seven weeks—or roughly 48% annualized. If ANT holds above $70, you keep the premium. If the stock is put to you, your effective purchase price drops to $65.20 — more than a 20% discount to the $83 IPO price, matching the exact drawdown SpaceX suffered. That would also put the entry price at a market cap of ~ $860 billion, or about 6.3x FY2027 anticipated revenues of 136.5 billion.
Cheap? No, but a lot cheaper than those who bought at the IPO.

articles.title_orig: The $2 trillion chip rally is getting wiped out — here's what history says comes next
articles.title_zh: The $2 trillion chip rally is getting wiped out — here's what history says comes next
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The biggest one-day rescue in stock market history is coming undone. Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia, and Wall Street's AI doubts are back with a vengeance.
Monday was supposed to be the start of the comeback. Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board brought Huang back at the White House's urging a week after chip stocks' worst week since 2001 , and the group added about $2 trillion in a day , a record $950 billion of it from Nvidia alone.
The sell-off since has hit the whole sector. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank nearly 8% Tuesday, with Micron ( MU ), AMD ( AMD ), and Intel ( INTC ) down roughly 8% to 11% and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) off about 4%. On Wednesday, the index briefly dropped below last Friday's low, as Nvidia and Micron fell as much as 9% and 13%, before buyers stepped in.
The pain spread Wednesday morning, when the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell more than 3% and the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) nearly 5%, with Alphabet ( GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) all lower. By the afternoon, dip buyers had nearly erased the S&P 500's loss.
Huang's return settled the question of who runs Nvidia. It didn't answer whether the debt-fueled AI-building boom will pay off, with tech borrowing costs climbing and the Fed still expected to raise rates on Dec. 9.
Sherwood News' Luke Kawa doesn't blame any single headline. "I think you can pin it on the sum of all the things that everyone's been pointing to for a while," he said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang Tuesday.
Washington wants to help. President Trump told the New York Post a pardon for Huang is " always an option , I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary." Asked about a government stake in Nvidia, he said, "It's probably not too late."
"I question what kind of a put it is," GammaRoad Capital Partners chief investment officer Jordan Rizzuto said. "I think it may be a very short-term put." Wednesday's new tariff proposal barely moved futures.
Turnaround Tuesday showed up on schedule. The next part of the script leans bearish. In the 20 times since 1993 that the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened a Monday 2% or more higher, it gave back at least half of that gain by Wednesday's close only five times, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. SPY came close to joining them Wednesday morning.
Every one of those fades went on to break the prior Friday's low within three months, most of them within a week. Of the 15 bounces that held up, only a third eventually broke the low in that span. Three of the drops came in the fall of 2008.
For the S&P 500, that low is about 6,883.
A year later, SPY was higher after 17 of those 20 big Monday rallies. In 2018, the Fed hiked into a nearly 20% drop and then paused, and stocks hit a record by April. Alfonso Peccatiello of the Macro Compass likes that echo but still sees more pain first, toward 6,500.
This Fed isn't in a position to blink . Wednesday's PCE report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed core prices up 3.3% from a year earlier, hotter than expected, making a December rate hike all but certain , with more possible early next year.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving. Advisors Capital Management's Gus Scacco expects Wall Street to wait on Huang's Senate testimony Dec. 3.
"We're going to probably be in purgatory here for a while," he said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang .

articles.title_orig: ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
articles.title_zh: ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Mathematics Álvaro Lozano-Robledo thought the Riemann hypothesis was out of AI’s reach for now. Credit: Bri Diaz/UConn Photo
The news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking. For months, reports have mounted of artificial-intelligence models toppling some of the toughest problems in mathematics , plunging the field into turmoil . But the latest claim was the most shocking yet: an AI model had helped to solve the field’s most famous open problem, the Riemann hypothesis .
AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?
AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?
The proof was released on 20 November by mathematician Levent Alpöge at AI giant Anthropic in San Francisco, California, who used an advanced version of the firm’s Claude model. It came in the form of 17 million lines of code in the open-source programming language Lean, which translates mathematical arguments into computer-certifiable code. In a matter of hours, a separate set of mathematicians rushed out a human-written proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which is in the branch of number theory and pertains to the randomness of prime numbers.
Alpöge’s proof has been independently verified by the non-profit organization behind Lean and the Mathlib Initiative, which runs the reference library of formalized mathematics results written in Lean. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him,” the community said in a statement on 21 November.
The mathematics community has broadly accepted the claim, although responses differ wildly. Some celebrate Alpöge’s achievement, but others see the development as proof that humans are fighting against machines for the future of mathematics .
Nature hears reactions from four mathematicians on what solving the Riemann hypothesis means to them.
Mathematician Tasmin Chu is part of the Association for Human Mathematics, whose members commit to doing AI-free research. Credit: Elizabeth Xiao
Tasmin Chu , PhD student in mathematics at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena.
A technology that can autonomously prove the Riemann hypothesis is no trivial matter. I think that it is imperative our society acts to pause AI development as soon as possible. Over the past year, mathematical institutions have faced the impossible task of adapting to the rapidly changing capabilities of AI in real time.
It’s enormously disruptive for early-career researchers — the people who are the intellectual future of our field. Soon other sectors of society will face the same issues.
My reaction is grave concern. AI companies urgently require democratic oversight. I do not think AI’s encroachment into math is inevitable, nor is the death of human mathematical practice inevitable. It’s a choice to disempower ourselves, just as it’s a choice to continue building these technologies despite grave safety concerns. I continue to practice mathematics without LLMs, because I believe it’s critical that scientific inquiry continues in the hands of human beings. Many of us at the Association for Human Mathematics — whose organizing committee I am on — are collectively making the same decision.
Harini Desiraju , postdoc in mathematics at the University of Warwick, UK.
Given the events of the past few months, this news wasn't entirely a surprise, but we need to wait to understand the Lean proof and let the experts verify it. It is several million lines of code, after all.
I am not a number theorist, so I might not have the same emotional attachment to the Riemann hypothesis. Nevertheless, I have deep appreciation for the ubiquity and the importance of the problem in several areas of maths and physics.
As for the recent events, I want to distinguish between formal proofs versus knowledge. It is an impressive feat to solve such a problem. However, because it is a Lean proof over millions of lines, it is going to take a while before the community gets real understanding, and validity of the proof. With an AI-independent approach available as well, it could present a great opportunity for discovery of new ideas and mathematics. We need to see how it all plays out.
There is another discussion to be had, which involves the role of frontier labs in research. Most of us see the potential benefits of this technology, but it is of utmost importance that we work towards a future where the agency is with the scientific community and not a couple of companies.
Mathematician Marcus Du Sautoy is anxious about what’s next for his field. Credit: David Levenson/Getty
Marcus Du Sautoy , m athematician and professor for the public understanding of science at the University of Oxford, UK.
It was real mix of emotions. A part of me says, how exciting to be alive when this great problem was solved! I think even when Fermat’s last theorem was solved, we had the same excitement and the same melancholy: that great motivator is gone.
Mixed in with that, is the complete surprise that it ended up being proved this way. If you’d asked me three months ago, I would never have predicted it.
There’s quite a lot of anxiety about what ‘math 2.0’ is going to look like .
Xin Zhang , assistant professor in mathematics at the University of Hong Kong.

articles.title_orig: China investigates Shanghai Party chief in latest blow to political elite - VOA
articles.title_zh: China investigates Shanghai Party chief in latest blow to political elite - VOA
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.
A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.
The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.
The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.
"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."
The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.
"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."
Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.
The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.
Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

articles.title_orig: Almost 2,000 migrants arrive on Spain’s Canary Islands in a single day, breaking a record
articles.title_zh: Almost 2,000 migrants arrive on Spain’s Canary Islands in a single day, breaking a record
articles.content_orig:
The Spanish Canary Islands witnessed a one-day migration record on Tuesday, with over 2,100 people arriving to the region in over 24 hours.
Most of the migrants landed on the the island of El Hierro, according to Spanish authorities.
"The Canaries can't take it anymore. We're experiencing an unprecedented migration pressure," President of the Canary Islands Fernando Clavijo wrote on X. He requested an urgent meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to discuss an immediate EU response.
Around 100 minors arrived on Tuesday, with a baby also born during the trip from Africa to the islands.
The Canaries, a tourist destination whose shortest gap with northwest Africa is around 100 kilometers (around 62 miles), tends to see more migrant arrivals in the fall when the waters are calmer. The waters become rougher in the winter due to storms and swells.
Earlier this month, nearly 1,600 migrants from West Africa were saved and taken to the Canary Islands in a previous record. Over 26,000 migrants came to the Canaries this year so far — with half of that figure in November alone.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The route from Africa to the Canaries is one of the deadliest in the world for migrants.
Boats taking off for the islands sometimes drift out to open sea, with the migrants onboard facing starvation, dehydration and lack of medical care. Human smugglers frequently organize the trips and abuse the migrants.
The spike in migration to the Canaries comes as Spain will hold a snap election on Sunday.
Migration, along with housing, will be one of the topics at the forefront of voters' minds when they cast their ballots.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who belongs to the center-left Socialist Party, has faced backlash from the opposition regarding his tolerant attitude towards migration. The Spanish government earlier this year enacted a plan to legalize up to 500,000 undocumented migrants.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In late July, over 80,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta, triggering a crisis for the Sanchez government. Countries such as Germany and Italy tightened or extended border controls due to the influx of migrants into Ceuta.
The far-right Vox party, which could receive its best-ever result in upcoming election, has called for Sanchez and his ministers to be prosecuted for treason over the Ceuta crisis. The conservative Popular Party could form a coalition government with Vox after the election.

Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC.
The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said.
The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said.
The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production.
The agreement would allow Europe to buy fuel such as diesel previously produced by Lukoil through the U.S.-led group rather than Russia.

articles.title_orig: Cutting-edge Nvidia chips not hard to find for sale in China, despite U.S. ban
articles.title_zh: Cutting-edge Nvidia chips not hard to find for sale in China, despite U.S. ban
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Patricia Zengerle and Simon Lewis
WASHINGTON, Nov 25(Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's intervention to save the career of Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang may have settled the question of who will run the world's most valuable chipmaker, but it has only intensified Washington's bigger fight over artificial intelligence, chips and China.
On Monday, Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive officer under pressure from Trump, a stunning reversal following ‌his resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
The decision drew applause from Wall Street. But it worried some US officials ‌and infuriated many lawmakers, both Democrats and some of Trump's fellow Republicans, who said Huang's return imperiled US security and called for tighter control of China's access to advanced chips used in artificial intelligence.
Nvidia stock fell almost 5% before the bell on Wednesday.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through ​both smuggling and remote access," said Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, in a social media post.
"The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."
Nvidia shares were down more than 7% on Tuesday after leaping on Monday on news of Huang's reinstatement.
His return to the helm of Nvidia has renewed the debate over how the US should compete in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
On one side are business figures close to Trump, including Jensen Huang, who have helped steer the administration to a more lenient policy. They contend that the best way to keep China from becoming an AI powerhouse is to sell it high-end American semiconductors, weakening Beijing's ‌incentive to learn how to make them itself.
On the other are China hawks in Congress ⁠and some parts of the administration, who want to choke off Beijing's access to the advanced chips that power the leading AI models and that only Nvidia and AMD produce.
Huang is due to be interviewed in Congress next week.
Since the news about his relationship with Alice Huang, and midterm elections that signaled voter unhappiness with the AI industry, US policy has become more hawkish. ⁠The Commerce Department on Monday added Megaspeed and several other firms to a trade blacklist, barring US companies from selling them chips and other technology.
Experts doubt that the Nvidia CEO's return will alter that course.
"I think it's going to lead to a tightening," said Aaron Friedberg, a professor of politics and international affairs at Princeton University. "There's going to be a lot of pressure from the Congress to tighten the existing restrictions."
Friedberg added: "This intervention by Trump, it's triggering what I think is going to be a much broader reaction, and it's not just ​going ​to be about Nvidia and it's not just going to be about China."
Trump celebrated his victory on Monday, taking credit for the ​turnaround in a long interview on CNBC and calling Huang a "national treasure."
"The board decided to ‌do what we wanted to do. And one of the things the board wanted to know: Is there a national security problem?" Trump said. "And after a lot of research ... we said, 'No, it's not a problem,'" he said.
Even before this week, Trump's administration had taken a conciliatory approach to China, reversing some restrictions on chip exports imposed under Democratic President Joe Biden.
Trump last December gave the green light to sales of Nvidia's advanced H200 AI chips to China, drawing criticism from both sides of the aisle.
Beyond the argument that allowing China to have Nvidia chips would make its tech industry dependent on US technology, there has been fear that tougher restrictions could prompt retaliation like extending a ban on exports of rare earth minerals used in electronics, AI hardware and military equipment.
Some analysts say China is keenly aware of the dangers of relying on US exports. "They want PRC companies using Huawei chips, not Nvidia chips. The real speed bump in selling chips to China recently has not been export ‌controls, essential as they are to protect sensitive technologies, but that they've been slow to buy," said Michael Schiffer, a senior fellow at the ​Center for American Progress.
In recent weeks, US authorities have taken a tougher approach, tightening licensing rules for some chip shipments and overseas data centers ​serving Chinese companies.
Three bills making their way through Congress would further tighten China's access to semiconductors: the ​AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress power over advanced chip exports, the Chip Security Act, which would require businesses to track their chips to combat smuggling, and the Match Act, which would ‌push US allies to restrict chipmaking equipment.
The Match Act in particular would be seen by ​Beijing as infringing on China's right to develop, a red line ​set out by Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Paul Triolo, tech policy lead at advisory firm DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, said.
"These would also be major breaches of the US-China truce, and Beijing will retaliate strongly to all of these measures, creating another dangerous tit-for-tat cycle of escalation that could undermine the truce and significantly worsen bilateral relations," he said.
Even if tightened restrictions on China do not pass before the end of 2026, Democrats will control large majorities ​in both the House of Representatives and Senate after January 3. With Republican China hawks, ‌they could pass bills with majorities large enough to override Trump's veto.
For their part, China's policymakers are unlikely to sit still.
"Beijing is unlikely to stake everything on Trump's goodwill and the next president," said Lizzi ​C. Lee, an expert on technology and the Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
"If anything, expect the push for domestic substitution to accelerate after this episode which already exposed the vulnerability of ​China's AI ambition."

articles.title_orig: They graduated college, but they haven’t been able to use their degrees
articles.title_zh: They graduated college, but they haven’t been able to use their degrees
articles.content_orig:
It's getting harder for college graduates to be optimistic about what's next after throwing their graduation caps in the air.
While unemployment among recent college graduates has been cooling as the job market has improved in the past few months, more and more graduates are having to settle for jobs that don't require the years of schooling they've just invested in. Based on data from the job-search platform Indeed, the share of bachelor's degree holders in jobs 12 months after graduation that don't require a college degree, or being underemployed, has risen dramatically in recent years.
Half of the class of 2025 were considered underemployed, above the 2017 to 2019 average of 39%.
Indeed economist Sneha Puri said the surge is due to the low-hire, low-fire job market that has been the story for the past few years. New grads also face a lot of competition for entry-level jobs. Puri said when employers do hire talent, they've been leaning on people "who can hit the ground running, as evident from the growth in job postings being driven by senior-level roles."
"That hits new graduates hardest, because they're most likely to apply for entry-level positions , which not only have seen job postings decline but also get several times as many applications as mid- and senior-level roles, including from people with more experience," Puri said.
Landing a job that doesn't require a college degree can be a short-term solution for new graduates, with long-term consequences.
"For workers who are underemployed or unemployed in their early years after graduating, that can have a stacking effect on their career over time, where they get knocked into a career trajectory that isn't as rewarding, isn't as engaging," Daniel Zhao, chief economist at Glassdoor, told Business Insider.
It could also affect their earning potential, as jobs that don't require degrees often pay less than those that do. For instance, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said there's no formal educational credential required to become a retail salesperson. That job paid an average annual wage of $37,310, per the latest 2025 BLS data, short of the overall average of $69,770. Software developers typically need a bachelor's degree, and Indeed said the average base salary for an entry-level software engineer in the US was about $82,000.
It can be tough to break free from underemployment.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"Seventy-three percent of graduates who start out underemployed remain so 10 years after completing college , making them at that point about 3.5 times more likely to be underemployed compared with those who start out in a college-level job," a 2024 report from the Burning Glass Institute and Strada Institute said.
Zhao said there's also a risk for employers if they hire a college grad who isn't engaged in their work duties or who would be a better fit in a different position.
It can be easier to find a job in your field depending on your major. The New York Fed found, based on Census Bureau data, that criminal justice, performing arts, and fine arts majors had the top three underemployment rates in 2024. Nursing, aerospace engineering, and civil engineering made up the bottom three.
While computer engineering was among the majors with low underemployment, this major had the second-highest unemployment rate.
Puri expects underemployment to remain elevated for the class of 2026. "An uptick would only reverse once employers again start to recognize the importance of hiring and investing in entry-level talent to train tomorrow's senior level experts," she said.
