articles.title_orig: China added nearly 10 times more power capacity than the US in 2025 as the AI race heats up
articles.title_zh: China added nearly 10 times more power capacity than the US in 2025 as the AI race heats up
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent.
"We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China.
The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research.
Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack."
Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging.
More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models.
Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday.
"He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said.
"Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China.
Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention.
For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China.
As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added.
Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations.
In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive.
Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country.
It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore.
Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups.
She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options.
"There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI."
However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.
She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company.
The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S.
A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years.
"The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers.
Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high.
Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work.
It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu.
He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

articles.title_orig: ASML’s CEO makes the case for selling chips to China

articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday accused Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang of violating federal laws limiting advanced technology exports to China .
In a post on X, Schumer said Huang "shipped extremely advanced chips to China, violating US export control law, in what amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the Space Race."
Nvidia and the White House did not immediately comment.
Schumer's statement marked an escalation of congressional criticism against Huang, who was reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday despite claims regarding his relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese government agent. Lawmakers from both parties are increasingly questioning Nvidia's trade with China, pressing for tighter controls while investigating whether Huang's conduct endangered national security.
Lawmakers have also faulted President Donald Trump for pushing Nvidia to reinstate Huang as CEO.
Schumer and other legislators insist Congress must act rapidly to curtail American chip sales to China. Senator Dave McCormick, a Pennsylvania Republican, said: "Congress must get to the bottom of what happened, and then strengthen our export controls to ensure China can't access our most advanced chips through the back door."
In a separate move on Tuesday, leading Democrats on four House committees wrote to Trump demanding answers about his awareness of Huang’s ties to the suspected agent.
"Your personal relationship with Mr. Huang and your willful blindness to the economic and national security risks posed by this scandal have put the American people at great risk," wrote Representatives Frank Pallone, Gregory Meeks, Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia, requesting all records of administration contact with the Nvidia board.
"Upon learning that Huang was in a relationship with a suspected agent of the Chinese government, what actions, if any, did Trump take to limit risks to America’s economic and national security?" the lawmakers inquired.
Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, told CNBC on Tuesday that more protections are needed on exports to China. "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang," he stated, adding it would be "just to make sure that he doesn't do something that is going to risk the United States."
Huang will appear on December 3 before the US Senate Banking Committee for a public hearing, panel's chair Tim Scott announced Monday.
Huang is also slated for a private briefing on December 1 with three House panels.
Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, said Huang's "reinstatement today at this juncture is a mistake." He noted: "We sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law. That is a dangerous precedent to set."

articles.content_orig:
A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.
Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday.
"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency.
Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.
The couple have two older children, aged five and seven.
"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."
In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true.
"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.
Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.
Heather Kutryk said her family had been preparing for years prior to her husband's mission, calling it "a long time coming"
Kutryk was the only Canadian selected to be part of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, where four astronauts are conducting scientific experiments and testing new technologies in space.
The crew also includes two US astronauts, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, and one Russian astronaut, Sergey Teteryatnikov.
Before their take off on 1 October, Heather Kutryk told Canada's public broadcaster CBC News that her family had been preparing for years before the mission, saying it was "a long time coming".
Heather added that her pregnancy was "not exactly planned" but that it was "a great thing".
"I'm not that stressed out. I feel like we have a really good community. I feel well supported by both CSA and Nasa," she said.
"It's six months, I feel like we'll be fine."
In a separate interview with BBC's US news partner CBS News, Joshua Kutryk said he hopes his new child will look at her dad's mission as "making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

articles.title_orig: Why this stock-market selloff is probably going to get worse before it gets better
articles.title_zh: Why this stock-market selloff is probably going to get worse before it gets better
articles.content_orig:
By The Premium Team – Nov 25, 2026 at 6:51AM EST
Investors have had a wild few days. On Friday, all three major U.S. indexes closed in correction territory, at least 10% below their recent highs. On Monday, the S&P 500 rose 4.7% and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.5%, both their best days since April 2025. The rally came after the board of Nvidia ( NVDA -4.46% ) reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. On Tuesday, the S&P 500 slipped 0.5%, its eighth loss in nine sessions, and the Nasdaq fell 1.48%. This morning, S&P 500 futures were down around 1% in pre-market trading, and Nasdaq-100 futures were down 1.61%.
So, have we seen the bottom?
Over the weekend, Motley Fool CEO and co-founder Tom Gardner pulled together a free, live Markets Special Report at short notice to help investors make sense of the sell-off. He was joined by TMF's chief investment officer Andy Cross and analysts from Team Hidden Gems and Team Rule Breakers. During Sunday evening's livestream, a member put that very question to the panel. The market will probably fall further at some point, Andy said. He just didn't know whether that would happen this year.
Team Rule Breakers' Jason Hall turned the question around. He asked members whether they had "structured your financial life so that this is a fun academic exercise." If you're living and dying by whether this is the bottom, he said, something else in your investing plan may need fixing.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Just look at Nvidia. On Sunday night, Huang was out as CEO, and the panel debated whether to buy more shares. Team Hidden Gems' Matt Frankel said the board should at least consider bringing him back. The next morning, it did, and the stock closed up 31%.
Big swings are normal. Andy pointed out that the market has historically fallen about 10% roughly once a year, 15% about every two years and 20% about every five years. It has also risen in about three years out of four.
As one member reminded the panel, quoting investor Peter Lynch, nobody rings a bell at the top or the bottom. So Tom suggests buying in a U shape. Don't try to pick the exact low. Keep adding a little at a time as prices fall and then recover.
A better question is whether your portfolio can cope with whatever comes next. Our investing principles can help.
None of this means the market can't fall further, or for longer. Tom pointed to Japan, where investors who bought at the 1989 peak were still sitting on losses more than 25 years later.
So what would worry the panel more? Matt would be concerned if company earnings slowed sharply. Andy pointed to inflation that won't go away. Jose said he'd watch for AI companies cutting back on data center spending. And Tom flagged signs that sales are getting weaker, such as customers taking longer to pay their bills. We'll be watching all four.
Potential Growth Indicator (PGI): Our PGI compares the cash sitting on the sidelines with the stock market's total value. It stood at 11.47% at the time of writing on Wednesday morning, up from 10.83% on Sunday. That puts it just above its long-run norm of about 11%. Historically, readings above 13% have been good times to buy. Readings near 10% or below point to more speculation.
VIX: The Cboe Volatility Index, or VIX, uses options prices to measure how much the S&P 500 is expected to swing over the next 30 days. It tends to jump when stocks fall. That's why it's often called Wall Street's "fear gauge." It was around 35 after Friday's sell-off. Tom noted that readings above 35 have often been attractive times to add to stocks. By Tuesday's close, it had eased to about 26.
Beta: You'll find this on any stock's TMF ticker page. It shows how volatile a stock is compared with the S&P 500. A stock with a beta of 2 tends to move about twice as much as the market, so expect it to fall harder in a sell-off.
Nobody knows if Friday was the low. This week showed how fast things can change. But if you hold some cash, own a broad mix of stocks and think in five-year stretches, you don't need to know. As Jason put it, the bottom then becomes a fun academic exercise.
When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor's total average return is 785 %* — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 200 % for the S&P 500.

articles.title_orig: Ladybird's new alpha shows there's life beyond Chromium
articles.title_zh: Ladybird's new alpha shows there's life beyond Chromium
articles.content_orig:
Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault .
After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it’s an installable package with automatic updating.
Ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google’s Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird’s rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. “The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,” project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday’s announcement. “The browser around it is modest, but functional.”
Nearly the entire modern web currently runs on three browser engines. There’s WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, Blink (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that’s where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.
An independent implementation of web standards has value not just by providing additional competition in the market, but because it can’t help but reveal places where sites depend on Chromium behaviors rather than published specifications. The fact that Ladybird exists isn’t likely to shift the market tides any time soon, but every new browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against, which can surface Chromium-specific assumptions and push the ecosystem toward the spec.
The Ladybird project was borne out of Kling’s SerenityOS project, an attempt to develop a new independent OS from scratch, before splitting off as a separate project. Kling formed the Ladybird Browser Initiative, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations. The project’s site highlights that there are no sponsored search engine deals supporting the project like many other popular browsers, and sponsoring entities have no say in the project roadmap.
The Ladybird alpha is a rolling release channel that updates automatically, and the downloadable package is a huge step to getting the browser onto the PCs of everyday users. “Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that,” Kling wrote. Though the browser began as C++, in keeping with the ethos of SerenityOS, the project has since started shifting toward Rust , starting with its JavaScript engine.
While it’s exciting to have a new engine option for browsing, the project leader notes that this is still a very early release. The browser build contains a built-in tool for reporting any websites that fail to render or crash the browser. Kling writes, “We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today.”
Microsoft users are still out in the cold on this one for now. The project says that future support for Windows is planned, but it’s macOS and Linux only for now.
I tested the Ladybird alpha version 2026.47.8 on my AceMagic W1 mini PC AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS with 16GB DDR5 and running Fedora Linux 44 with the new KDE Plasma 6.8.3 , and the most surprising thing about the alpha build was how little it feels like alpha software.
The browser seemed to handle most anything I threw at it without issue. Day-to-day tabbed browsing mechanics felt snappy and normal. A 50MB test video file downloaded quickly and smoothly. With a dozen tabs open, switching between them was instant, and the browser felt responsive throughout. Options menus were surprisingly fleshed out for a build this young.
Google Maps loaded instantly, located me, and handled everything I threw at it: adding and removing layers, zooming out from the Midwest, and dropping into Street View in Alberta, Canada in around three seconds. Everything rendered fast enough that my mini PC’s fan spun up noticeably. GitHub’s site, including repository navigation, worked without a hitch. So did YouTube and the news sites I tried.
I could stall the browser, but it took some effort. With about 10 tabs open, I was streaming a 4K test video file from my personal Jellyfin server. Everything worked fine at first, but after skipping around in the file over and over again, the browser eventually got stuck. Mind you, this is an alpha build that I was trying to trip up, not a representation of something inherently broken.
After spending an evening with Ladybird, I can say that while it won’t be replacing Firefox for me anytime soon, I was genuinely impressed that a scratch-made engine could perform this well in such an early state. Most new browser projects are forks of something that already exists. Ladybird is the rare exception, an engine written from nothing, and the alpha runs well enough that if you have a Mac or Linux PC handy, it’s worth downloading a build and poking around yourself. Just remember Kling’s warning: This is nowhere near trustworthy enough to make your daily driver, yet.
What the alpha demonstrates is that a small team of independent developers, funded by donations, has built a browser engine from scratch that handles real web browsing without a fuss. That it works this well this soon, using no existing engine code, is an achievement. I thought I was a Firefox loyalist, but I’ll be keeping an eye on where this one goes.

articles.title_orig: China launches Shenzhou 24 spacecraft carrying 2 Chinese and 1 Pakistani astronaut
articles.title_zh: China launches Shenzhou 24 spacecraft carrying 2 Chinese and 1 Pakistani astronaut
articles.content_orig:
Islamabad, Pakistan — It was 5:18am (00:18 GMT) on Wednesday, before dawn in a chilly Islamabad. On the screen at the front of the auditorium, a Chinese rocket carrying Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, Pakistan’s first astronaut, rose on a column of orange flames.
As the rocket lifted off, Pakistan’s national anthem began. The audience, which had been slouching in their seats, rose row by row and sang along.
While many took out their phones to record the historic moment, Zainab Abbasi’s eyes remained fixed on the giant screen.
“I had my phone out to record it on video, but I was so caught up in the moment that I forgot to record, and I was just standing there with my phone closed,” Abbasi, 21, told Al Jazeera.
A second-year undergraduate student of physics and astronomy at the National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST), Abbasi was with her friends in the auditorium at the headquarters of the Pakistan Space & Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO).
As the rocket climbed higher, the hall erupted in applause and chants of “Pakistan Zindabad” (“Long live Pakistan”).
The Long March-2F rocket lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China, carrying Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, alongside Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan Air Force pilot.
But within two minutes of liftoff, the hall fell silent. No one spoke. Faces across the rows were tense. On the screen, the rocket had shrunk to a dot.
“There was, I think, anticipation and also, for me specifically, a sort of, you know, underlying anxiety,” Abbasi told Al Jazeera.
On January 28, 1986, the US space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff, killing all seven crew members.
About 10 minutes after Wednesday’s launch, the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft separated from the rocket and entered orbit, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA).
The silence lasted several minutes, until one of the hosts congratulated the audience on a successful launch. People got up, greeted one another or headed for the doors.
A few hours later, CMSA and SUPARCO confirmed that the spacecraft had docked at China’s Tiangong space station at 8:56am (03:56 GMT). The crew were expected to enter the station at about 11:45am (06:45 GMT).
The auditorium had been packed by 5am (00:00 GMT). Those unable to find a seat sat on the floor or stood along the walls.
Taiba Riaz, a final-year mathematics student at NUST, said every seat was taken when she arrived at about 4:20am (23:20 GMT Tuesday). Originally from Chitral in Pakistan’s northwest, she lives in a university hostel.
When she asked hostel authorities to leave early in the morning, she said they asked where she was going. “I was like, ‘I am going to witness a history,’” she said, giggling.
Many in the auditorium held glossy cards bearing Ali’s portrait in a spacesuit and the words “Pakistan’s First Manned Space Mission”. Paper flags of Pakistan and China rested on laps, while green and white balloons lined the stage.
The screen carried a livestream of the launch. There was a brief moment of hilarity when, just before liftoff, a YouTube advertisement appeared, causing mild panic that the critical moment might be missed.
Abbasi, the second-year student, had been at SUPARCO since 2am (21:00 GMT Tuesday). She lives 40km (25 miles) away and had left home at 7pm (14:00 GMT) on Tuesday to spend the night at her aunt’s house nearby.
She is a member of PakAstronomers, a group of amateur astronomers in Islamabad. Her interest in astronomy began around 2018, when she was 13, after the cartoon series Beyblade introduced her to constellations.
Her family, particularly her father, has always supported her, even if they do not always understand her passion, she said.
“When I was a child and interested in space, becoming an astronaut felt like a far-off dream only available to a child in America and not in Pakistan,” she said.
Ahzam Farogh, a physics undergraduate at NUST and vice president of the society, used to wake at 3am to watch rocket launches.
“My parents used to ask, ‘What is there in this?’ like it will never be us,” he said.
Adan Athar, a second-year space sciences student at the Institute of Space Technology (IST) in Islamabad, is from Faisalabad and a founding member of the Faisalabad Astronomical Society.
She told Al Jazeera she was the first in her family to take an interest in space.
“Yes, they were very supportive, and they think I will be the next astronaut,” she said with a shy smile.
But it is not only Pakistan’s youth following Ali’s journey.
Saif-ul-Islam Qureshi, a 72-year-old electronics engineer, has been watching the sky for at least 50 years.
“I was 12 years old when I started this hobby with my small binocular, and then my first observation was the Big Dipper in the sky,” he told Al Jazeera.
The Big Dipper is a group of seven bright stars whose two end stars point towards the North Star.
Qureshi helped found PakAstronomers, the group Abbasi belongs to. It was initially called the Pakistan Astronomy Society.
Its members took astronomy to schools, colleges, universities and public parks. Many people did not know planets could be seen with the naked eye, he said.
Over the past decade, however, that had changed. Even small children were now well informed.
“We were sensing that a storm was building. A storm is building, and a storm in a positive sense,” he said.
In a speech before the launch, SUPARCO chairman Muhammad Yousaf Khan said Pakistan was setting its sights further ahead.
“Our ambition is beyond just this launch. Our commitment is to reach the moon by 2035,” he said.
Speaking to Al Jazeera afterwards, Khan said the first step would be a lunar rover, due to fly in 2028.
“If the Chinese people have reached here, there is no shortcoming in us. I believe one day, we too will reach that stage, if we keep moving step by step,” Khan told Al Jazeera.
Farogh, the NUST physics undergraduate, said collaboration with China could help Pakistan avoid having to build its space capabilities from scratch.
“If we have this collaboration, I think it’s good that we can use the already built-up platforms of China and utilise them to do something further. By making our own satellites, and through our own astronauts, we can go towards some further research,” he told Al Jazeera.
For Qureishi, the veteran astronomer, that excitement for the future climaxed when Ali took off.  That moment, he said, was about much more than Ali.
“It is not Zeeshan [in the astronaut’s seat]. It is Pakistan’s young generation sitting there,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Libyan naval officers die following Ukrainian drone attack, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Libyan naval officers die following Ukrainian drone attack, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Former White House official Morgan Murphy says Ukraine’s strike on Russian warship in Libya signals major shift in war.
The Libyan National Army (LNA) has vowed to retaliate after a Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian warship moored at a Benghazi port killed two Libyan soldiers.
"With deep sadness and sorrow, and with hearts believing in the decree and destiny of Allah, the General Command of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces mourns two of its heroic sons belonging to the Naval Forces General Staff," the LNA wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday.
Calling the Ukrainian attack "sinful aggression," the LNA also quoted the Quran, writing, "And those who have wronged are going to know to what [kind of] return they will be returned."
RUSSIA WARNS OF 'PREVENTIVE NUCLEAR ATTACK' AS MEDVEDEV CLAIMS UKRAINE, NATO CROSSED LINE
The LNA said the soldiers, identified as Al-Taher Abdullah al-Sadiq and Lieutenant Ali Mohammed al-Said, died Tuesday from injuries sustained during the Sunday attack.
A satellite image shows a capsized and burning Russian naval ship and the northern port area after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base, which Libya's eastern-based government said was caused by a suspected drone attack, in Benghazi, Libya, November 22, 2026. (Vantor/Handout via REUTERS)
Libya's eastern government, the Government of National Stability, was joined by the country's U.N.-recognized western government, the Government of National Unity, based in the capital, Tripoli, in criticizing the attack.
US CALLS TURKEY-LIBYA MARITIME DEAL 'UNHELPFUL AND PROVOCATIVE' AMID REGIONAL BACKLASH
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of the Government of National Unity has expressed its condemnation and denunciation of statements made by the Ukrainian President regarding the execution of military operations targeting Russian naval vessels in the vicinity of the city of Benghazi," the Ministry wrote in a statement.
The Tripoli-based government also denied accusations that the Ukrainian attack was launched from Libyan territorial waters.
FRENCH TROOPS SECRETLY DEPLOYED INSIDE UKRAINE AS EX-NATO CHIEF PRAISES MACRON'S 'GUTS'
"The Ministry categorically rejects the conduct of any foreign military operations within Libyan territory or its territorial waters," it added.
Despite the denial, Libya's eastern government requested an investigation into the possibility that the drone strike was launched from Western Libya, citing information that Ukrainian military could be present in "areas around Misrata, Zawiya and other potential locations," according to news outlet Al Arabiya.
NATO FIGHTER JET CLEARED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN MISSILE OVER POLAND AS WARSAW PUSHES FOR US TROOPS
Western Libya's government criticized the Benghazi-based eastern government for hosting Russian ships in the first place.
"Hosting illicit foreign forces and granting them access to national facilities invites the spillover of external conflicts into the country," Tripoli said, according to Al Arabiya.
A satellite image shows a capsized and burning Russian naval ship and the northern port area after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base, which Libya's eastern-based government said was caused by a suspected drone attack, in Benghazi, Libya, November 22, 2026. (Vantor/Handout via REUTERS)
The Benghazi-based LNA is the military arm of Libya's eastern government, one half of the ruling party in the North African nation. Following the fall of former Libyan dictator Muammar Qadaffi, rivaling power factions made claims on ruling the nation.
The United Nations-backed western government counts the U.S. and European Union among its supporters. The eastern government is broadly aligned with Russia and is not formally recognized by the U.N.
Russia supported Libya's vow for revenge.
"Well, certainly, no state will leave an attempt on the lives of its servicemen unpunished," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in a video.
Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov moderates Russian President Vladimir Putin's annual special televised question-and-answer session and year-end news conference, held at the Gostiny Dvor trade and exhibition center in Moscow, Russia, on December 19, 2025. (Sefa Karacan/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Ukraine , while confirming the strike, claimed it was self-defense.
"Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine's actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a message posted to Telegram.
Sybiha also said that the ships it attacked — Russian naval vessels and cargo ships transporting military equipment — were valid military targets as defined by the United Nations Charter's Article 51.
"Ukraine is not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," Sybiha added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also confirmed a separate drone strike on a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
articles.title_zh: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_orig: U.S. economy grew at rapid 4.3% pace in third quarter, new estimate shows
articles.title_zh: U.S. economy grew at rapid 4.3% pace in third quarter, new estimate shows
articles.content_orig:
The US economy boomed last quarter, growing at an annualized rate of 4.3%, the Commerce Department reported on Wednesday. That’s a massive jump from the 3.4% rate initially reported. Both figures take inflation into account.
Business investment, boosted by software spending, was the single biggest driver of the third-quarter surge, a sign of major AI-related spending. Consumer spending, which accounts for three quarters of gross domestic product, also played a key role in delivering the best quarter of economic growth in three years.
But that robust growth comes with an inflation complication. In separate data released Wednesday, the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge — showed prices accelerated slightly to an annualized rate of 3.8% in October from 3.7% the prior month. That’s almost double the Fed’s target of 2%, solidifying the case for a rate hike next month.
On a monthly basis, price increases slowed to 0.3% from 0.5% in September.
The booming economy isn’t translating into increased wealth for many Americans, whose savings have dwindled as income growth has slowed.
While Wednesday’s PCE report showed that the personal savings rate (savings as a percentage of after-tax income) rose 0.5 percentage points to 4.1%, it’s below the 4.9% rate seen in October of last year. The increase in savings came from a boost in after-tax income growth last month, though much of that was tied to Medicare rebate payments.
But in a potentially worrisome sign for the economy, Americans are reining in their spending: When stripping out the 0.3% monthly price increase, spending was flat for October.
“The cautious consumer is back. It will be a bargain-hunting holiday for many Americans,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote in a note Wednesday.
CNN’s Alicia Wallace contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: The AI trade is unraveling days after Jensen Huang's comeback sparked a monster rally
articles.title_zh: The AI trade is unraveling days after Jensen Huang's comeback sparked a monster rally
articles.content_orig:
The AI trade was unraveling on Wednesday, just days after a parabolic rally sparked by Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
US stocks barreled toward another losing session the day before Thanksgiving, as the global stock rally triggered by Huang's comeback fizzled out. The Nasdaq 100 was down nearly 4% and the S&P 500 fell 3%.
The move attests to how temperamental the AI trade has become, with big events like Huang's return and the Anthropic IPO unable to lift sentiment and restart the bull rally. Chips, neoclouds, and hypserscalers were all down sharply on Wednesday.
Nvidia dropped 9%, and remains down more than 30% from its early October high. Anthropic, however, made a remarkable round-trip move during the session, dropping as much as 10% but turn positive in afternoon trading. Shares of the Claude maker were up back above their IPO price around 1 p.m. ET, trading around $85.
Dell , notably, dropped 8%, despite reporting blockbuster results for the third quarter after the bell on Tuesday.
"Dell just put up one of the best quarters of the AI cycle, and the stock barely moved, yet another sign that the market is 'over' the AI trade," Luke Lango, an independent tech analyst, wrote in a note. "That's the AI transition period in a nutshell: the fundamentals are booming, but the market is pricing in a slowdown that hasn't shown up in the numbers yet."

Here were the most notable moves in the tech sector in the US:

Meanwhile, hot inflation data and the prospect of additional tariffs from the Trump administration were adding to the selling pressure.
Analysts had been mulling whether Monday's relief rally was a dead-cat bounce , a short-lived recovery in stocks before the market makes its way to a new low.
A few worries appear to have triggered the latest bout of selling:
Doubts have been swirling around Nvidia's future , given the ongoing investigation into Huang and uncertainty that continues to loom over the firm's future financing deals and business in China .
"Perception is important, and the current perception of Nvidia's board is not the one that the world's leading chip designer should want," David Morrison, a senior market analyst at Trade Nation, said about Huang's reinstatement in a client note.
Huang is scheduled to testify before the US Senate Banking Committee on December 3 about US chip-export controls, amid mounting congressional scrutiny of Nvidia.
Huang's reinstatement has not removed the political uncertainty surrounding AI, Macquarie Group strategists warned.
"That's because with Huang at Nvidia or not, it's safe to say that the politicians are still 'coming after' AI," they wrote.
Investors are growing anxious that the AI boom is starting to crumble . The market has pent-up anxiety about the trajectory of capex spending , and any hint that firms are either spending too little or too much on AI has triggered a wave of panic-selling recently.
"There is a sense of caution on the markets, with investors not quite sure if they should go all-in on tech again, or whether Monday's Nvidia-fuelled tech rally was a one-day affair," Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said in a morning note.
The prospect of additional tariffs is rattling investors . Reports circulated this week that the Trump administration is readying to unveil a new slate of levies on China and other trading partners this week. It also puts the spotlight on inflation and the likelihood that rates will move higher, a headwind for stocks.
"The threat of another wave of tariffs by Donald Trump could cause unease, particularly if they are seen to cause new inflationary pressures," Coatsworth added, referring to news reports that the Trump administration is preparing to impose fresh taxes on imports from China and other trading partners.
Wall Street is eyeing the possibility that selling will continue for the foreseeable future.
JPMorgan analysts said they were flipping from a tactically bullish to a "Tactically Cautious" view on stocks, pointing to uncertainty around Nvidia in particular.
"In hindsight, it seems obvious that we should have been on the sidelines but we, similar to the market, had viewed NVDA and capital markets activity as the necessary support for Tech to form a bottom and thus whiffed on the tactical bullish call," the bank's market intelligence team wrote in a client note. "Now, the uncertainty surrounding NVDA and peers and opacity over 2028 and beyond makes Tech longs highly uncertain in the very near-term."
Fundstrat's Newton said near-term market trends looked "negative." He said he was searching for signs that tech stocks were starting to gain an edge over defensives, which could happen in the next two weeks, due to seasonal patterns in the market.
"Until that leadership starts to roll over, it's difficult to have conviction that risk appetite has returned in a meaningful way," he said.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia leads tech sell-off as Huang comeback rally fizzles and AI concerns return
articles.title_zh: Nvidia leads tech sell-off as Huang comeback rally fizzles and AI concerns return
articles.content_orig:
Technology stocks fell on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's return faded and failed to calm concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1% and traded off its lows, recovering from steeper losses earlier in the session. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector edged down 2%.
"We just feel that this is panic right now," Venu Krishna, head of U.S. equity strategy at Barclays, told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday.
"What the market is telling you is that the AI growth narrative has hit a wall and given the centrality of that theme at the economic level, the market is expecting some sort of a macro shock," he added.
After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 5% Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices , Marvell Technology and Intel all dropped about 2%, with some plunging further. Micron Technology declined 5%.
Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday briefly revived appetite for tech stocks but didn't fully calm investor concerns over the high costs tied to the AI build-out and worries of a potential slowdown.
Other stocks tied to the AI trade also plummeted. Oracle fell more than 4%. CoreWeave and Nebius moved lower.
AI lab Anthropic bucked the sell-off, however, and climbed more than 4% after shares dropped below last week's blockbuster IPO price.
Wednesday's declines also came as Wall Street digested a hot inflation reading that fueled concerns that higher interest rates could dent demand for growth stocks, including tech.
Amazon , Tesla and Alphabet each declined about 2%. Microsoft lost more than 1% and Meta traded higher.

articles.title_zh: FAA’s ‘line up and wait’ rule is in effect: How it could affect your flight
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong

The Federal Aviation Administration has restricted a takeoff protocol that could potentially slow holiday travel. The FAA has modified the "line up and wait" procedure that allows departing planes to taxi to a runway and remain in queue for takeoff. The maneuver helps expedite flight operations but has been revised due to staffing concerns.
The change took effect Tuesday, Nov. 24, as an estimated 417,000 flights began to take to the air for the nine-day Thanksgiving travel period. Under the stricter guidelines, a dedicated air traffic control supervisor must be available to coordinate line up and wait operations, rather than having air traffic controllers multitask.
"The purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements," the FAA notice said. The enhanced policy ensures that a supervisor or controller is "fully available to oversee the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks."
The stricter guidance could impact takeoff operations at understaffed facilities, and is slated to remain in effect until June 9, 2027.
Read more: What you're entitled to when flights are delayed or canceled
Related: Best travel credit cards
Brian Cohen, a travel writer at " The Gate ," said that "the timing of the rule being placed into effect could have been better, as it could cause delays and even cancellations of flights during the busiest travel period of the year."
Adding the FAA's decision to enforce the rule to the pressing holiday crowds, the threat of bad weather in large swaths of the nation, and recent technical glitches, all increase "the chances of your travel plans being interrupted," Cohen wrote.
He suggests travelers frequently check the latest flight updates during the holiday rush.
On Monday, a temporary ground stop at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport was blamed on a staffing shortage. More than 170 flights were delayed as the Thanksgiving travel season began.
The FAA launched a recruitment campaign this year to bolster staffing, with an estimated 1,500 positions currently unfilled. An expected loss of 5,307 controllers is forecast over the next three years due to attrition, the agency says.
Read more: When to buy travel insurance (and when it's too late)
In a statement Tuesday regarding holiday travel, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said that government officials are working to "predict and address congestion in the airspace" and have "taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations."
The FAA recommends that air travelers check nasstatus.faa.gov for real-time airport conditions to see how weather may affect their flights. The Department of Transportation also provides information related to airline policies regarding delays and flight cancellations .

articles.title_orig: FAA Investigates Amazon Drone Crash in Michigan
articles.title_zh: FAA Investigates Amazon Drone Crash in Michigan
articles.content_orig:
A drone making a delivery for the online retailer Amazon crashed outside of Detroit on Friday after delivering a bottle of shampoo and now the Federal Aviation Administration is investigating.
The uncrewed vehicle successfully delivered the package to Jim Brennan’s Huntington Woods, Michigan, backyard shortly after his wife placed the order, he told CNN affiliate WXYZ .
“She ordered shampoo, and we just expected a truck to pull up, and then we get the notifications it’s coming by drone in seven minutes,” Brennan said.
The package was left in the backyard, but as he watched the Prime Air drone taking off, it hit a fiberoptic cable and knocked off a propeller.
“All of a sudden I realized it’s under a wire. It’s going to come up under that wire. And it did. And when it caught that, it just, it went crazy,” he said. “Like a sick bird, it tried to get out of here, but it couldn’t.”
Video recorded by Claire Brennan, who is not related to Jim Brennan, shows the aircraft struggling to fly before wobbling out of control and crashing as she walked by.
The drone landed on Logan Coomes’ garage next door, which he said had some minor damage.
“There’s a little corner on the tip of the peak of the garage where I think if it did rain, water would get through right now,” he told WXYZ. “Some shingles were flapped up from their original positions.”
No one was injured in the crash, Amazon said in a statement to CNN. The company removed the damaged drone from Coomes’ garage and is in contact with him.
“Safety is our top priority and incidents are extremely rare,” Jack Stelzner, an Amazon spokesperson, said. “Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service.”
Prime Air drones have delivered hundreds of thousands of packages this year and nearly 6,000 are flown a day, Amazon said.
The “highly autonomous” MK30 drones can deliver items weighing five pounds or less, including groceries, cosmetics, medicine and electronics to the area surrounding their bases, the company said.
Locations are limited, but in August Amazon announced plans to reach nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of the year, a six-fold increase. The company plans to reach half a billion customers a year by the end of the decade.
The MK30 drones are designed to have a “best-in-class perception system to detect and avoid obstacles,” according to the company, and “navigate around obstacles like trampolines or clotheslines that may not have been captured in satellite imagery.”
Still, there have been crashes.
Last fall, Amazon ordered a brief halt to drone flights after two of its MK30 aircraft collided with a crane outside of Phoenix. No one was injured but the drones sustained substantial damage.
“We’ve completed our own internal review of this incident and are confident that there wasn’t an issue with the drones or the technology that supports them,” Terrence Clark, an Amazon spokesperson, told CNN at the time. “Nonetheless, we’ve introduced additional processes like enhanced visual landscape inspections to better monitor for moving obstructions such as cranes.”
CNN’s Alexandra Skores contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: North Korea Kicks Out Swiss Diplomats in Spat Linked to Ukraine War
articles.title_zh: North Korea Kicks Out Swiss Diplomats in Spat Linked to Ukraine War
articles.content_orig:
The Swiss government has said it regretted North Korea’s decision to close Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang in a spat over sanctions just weeks after Bern reopened its office in the North Korean capital.
Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said it was officially informed earlier on Wednesday of the North Korean authorities’ decision to close the Swiss diplomatic office.
On Tuesday, North Korea condemned Switzerland for adding a children’s camp to its sanctions list over Western allegations that it was involved in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine and said it would consider shutting down the diplomatic office in Pyongyang.
“The [foreign ministry] regrets this decision and is arranging for the Head of the Office to return to the Embassy of Switzerland in Beijing,” the Swiss ministry said in a statement.
North Korea ordered the envoy to leave within 48 hours, its Foreign Ministry said.
In a statement carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the ministry said the move was in response to Switzerland’s decision to impose sanctions on North Korea’s Songdowon International Children’s Camp, calling it an overtly hostile act.
Pyongyang’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the head of the diplomatic office, Sylvain Astier, and handed him a memorandum urging him to close the office, KCNA said.
“The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea [DPRK] declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours,” KCNA said, using the country’s official name.
“Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us,” it said.
The expulsion comes less than a month after Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis formally reopened the diplomatic office in Pyongyang.
The sanctions infringed on North Korea’s sovereignty by denying what was its obligation to provide children with opportunities for culture and recreation, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s influential sister, Kim Yo Jong, said.
Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs defended its sanctions policy on Tuesday, saying it was independent of the reopening of the diplomatic office, which it said was carried out “in line with our universalist foreign policy”.
“Its aim is to maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues,” it told the Reuters news agency.
Over the weekend, Kim Jong Un personally received credentials from the new ambassadors of 10 countries, including Russia and Sweden, in a rare diplomatic ceremony in Pyongyang.
Kim said North Korea sought to expand foreign relations with countries that respected its sovereignty, but would oppose attempts to restrict the independent rights and right to development of sovereign states.
Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country. Both Kim Jong Un and Kim Yo Jong reportedly attended school in Switzerland as teenagers in the 1990s.
Meanwhile, North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for aid and military technology transfers.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic is getting more AI from less compute. That's great for Anthropic and bad for everyone else.
articles.title_zh: Anthropic is getting more AI from less compute. That's great for Anthropic and bad for everyone else.
articles.content_orig:
A little-known concept called the "compute multiplier" is raising a potentially trillion-dollar question about the AI boom .
What if AI becomes so efficient that companies don't need nearly as many data centers, chips, and power plants as investors expect?
That's a concern emerging in financial markets following revelations from Anthropic , the company behind the most powerful AI models. It's adding pressure on the AI trade as some investors rethink their bets on the technology.
In its IPO filing , Anthropic explained how it's finding ways to get more out of the computing power it already has.
The company calls these advances "compute multipliers" — breakthroughs that allow its AI systems to accomplish more work using less computing power. Anthropic says these improvements are helping it deliver more value to customers and generate more revenue from its existing computing infrastructure.
That's great for Anthropic. But it has potentially enormous implications for the AI industry's spending plans .
Investors have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into companies building data centers, making chips, and supplying electricity to power the AI revolution.
Much of that investment is based on forecasts of how quickly AI revenue will grow, and how much computing power will be needed to support that growth.
AI demand remains strong. But what if those compute forecasts are wrong?
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Charles Zvibleman, VP of strategic finance at AlphaSense, recently suggested on X that concerns about future AI infrastructure demand can potentially be traced to what Anthropic discussed with potential investors in the weeks leading up to its IPO.
According to Zvibleman, Anthropic told investors it could generate four times as much revenue from a given amount of computing power as previously expected, with further efficiency gains anticipated.
If AI companies can generate significantly more revenue from the same computing power, they could meet user demand and achieve their financial targets with less infrastructure than investors previously anticipated.
Anthropic's IPO filing describes how its researchers are finding ways to train and operate increasingly powerful AI systems more efficiently.
The company also explains how Claude itself is helping researchers develop better versions of the technology , potentially accelerating these improvements.
The company specifically highlighted this efficiency gain in its filing.
"Our researchers have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference — reducing the compute required to serve a given level of model performance," it wrote. "This allows us to provide greater value for customers and generate greater revenue from our compute base over time."
This doesn't mean demand for AI is weakening. Quite the opposite. Anthropic says customer demand continues to exceed the computing capacity it has available.
But there's a difference between demand for AI services and demand for the physical infrastructure needed to deliver them.
And some investors are questioning whether the two will grow as closely together as previously assumed.
That brings us to memory chips .
Memory prices have long been an early indicator of changes in the technology industry and, sometimes, the broader economy.
Prices soared earlier during the AI boom as companies raced to build computing infrastructure. Now they're falling.
According to data compiled by Bloomberg, prices for one benchmark NAND flash memory chip are well below their highs from earlier this year. Prices for a benchmark DRAM memory chip have also slipped.
The declines don't prove that Anthropic's breakthroughs are responsible. Memory prices respond to many factors, including production levels, inventories, and demand from consumer electronics manufacturers.
Still, the timing is intriguing.
For years, investors have been betting that AI will require ever-growing amounts of computing power.
Anthropic's compute multiplier raises a different possibility: AI could keep growing spectacularly while needing considerably less hardware than expected.
That's a potentially uncomfortable thought for companies supplying the AI boom.

articles.title_orig: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours
articles.title_zh: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours
articles.content_orig:
Colombian security forces have freed around 76 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena.
Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 local time (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella described as a failed attempt at robbing an armoured car carrying money.
They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway.
With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, de la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, killing one gunman.
Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.
Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage-takers. Four have been arrested.
De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".
He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation personally. He could be seen flanked by the commanders of the operation with a handgun strapped to his belt, in footage released following its conclusion.
De la Espriella said the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in but had refused.
Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of the hostages, among them elderly women.
But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, located in a popular shopping centre.
Local media report that, as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.
De la Espriella said they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob a cash-laden armoured car had been foiled.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
Johan Correa, one of the rescued hostages, described to local media how the gunmen, who he said had been disguised, had entered the supermarket, where he worked.
"We had just started our shift when some guys dressed as police officers came in and started robbing the place," he said. "They were robbers, but we thought they were police."
He added that he and other hostages had been locked in a cold storage room, face down with their hands tied.
"We were there for more than four hours, lying on the floor with our hands tied, and it was a really tough experience."
Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, told Caracol radio that the assailants wore masks and had been armed with guns and knives.
Velázquez said the gunmen repeatedly threatened the hostages, telling them that they had rigged the exits with explosives.
He said that "thank God" they had been rescued, describing moments of tension as they heard explosions and a helicopter flying above.
Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people kneel with their hands behind their heads.
It is unclear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers.
Local media report that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded.
The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.
The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.
Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces.
A woman called Sandra told Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage.
Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.
Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.
But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police said they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.
At one point, flights into the city were halted, with planes diverted to Barranquilla.
Special forces, including units specialised in dealing with kidnappings, were deployed to Cartagena, a popular destination among foreign and Colombian tourists.
Cartagena's Mayor Dumek Turbay called for calm but the granddaughter of one of the hostages told Colombian newspaper El Tiempo that "this shows we're not safe anywhere".
De la Espriella was elected earlier this year on a promise to crack down on Colombia's criminal groups.
He had travelled to the central city of Villavicencio to inspect the damage caused by a car bomb that detonated outside the regional government's offices on Tuesday.
While de la Espriella blamed the leader of a dissident rebel group for that attack, he was adamant that the hostage takers were "simple bandits" without political affiliations.

articles.title_orig: Court casts heavy doubt over most serious Netanyahu charges, in huge blow to prosecution
articles.title_zh: Court casts heavy doubt over most serious Netanyahu charges, in huge blow to prosecution
articles.content_orig:
Benjamin Netanyahu called for his trial to be ended "immediately"
Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.
The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.
They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.
Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".
"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.
"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."
Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.
The case now under serious doubt, known as Case 4,000, concerns an alleged "reciprocal arrangement" between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder in Israel's biggest telecoms company. Both denied any wrongdoing.
In a highly unusual step, a judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Wednesday to express their concerns.
"The chances of conviction are low â to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, Israeli media reported.
The judges also cast doubt on whether Netanyahu's actions, which are subject to a second case â concerning another alleged quid-pro-quo with another media baron, known as Case 2,000 â met the threshold for criminality.
While they left open the possibility of a conviction in the third case: Case 1,000, which alleges Netanyahu acted for the benefit of an Australian billionaire after being gifted cigars and champagne by him.
Netanyahu: What are the corruption charges?
However, the judges told the attorney general that, in the public interest, there needed to be a "rethink" in how the trial should move forward, Israeli media report.
Baharav-Miara said she would consider the judges' recommendations.
It has been six years since Netanyahu became Israel's first sitting prime minister to face a criminal trial.
He has always claimed to be the victim of a political witch-hunt and said on Wednesday that the "fabricated cases" against him were now falling apart.
The cases have continued to progress in court while Netanyahu remained in power throughout the war in Gaza, though judges agreed to reduce the number of hearings due to security concerns around the conflict.
The accusations against him have rocked Israeli politics, fuelling already deep divisions. His trial has coincided with controversial, far-reaching judiciary reforms by Netanyahu's government.
For his opponents, Netanyahu's fear of prison has distorted his decision-making as prime minister and made him especially dependent on his far-right coalition partners to remain in power.
This latest development will give a boost to Netanyahu, whose political opponent Gadi Eisenkot is currently attempting to form a coalition government after an inconclusive general election last month.
While Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats than that of his rival, both fell short of an outright majority. Israel's president has offered Eisenkot the first chance to form a new administration.
Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.

articles.content_orig:
Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC.
The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said.
The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said.
The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production.
The agreement would allow Europe to buy fuel such as diesel previously produced by Lukoil through the U.S.-led group rather than Russia.

articles.title_orig: Young Britons’ sex lives have fallen off a cliff, major survey shows
articles.title_zh: Young Britons’ sex lives have fallen off a cliff, major survey shows
articles.content_orig:
London — One-third of Brits between the ages of 16 and 24 have never had sex, according to a large-scale, periodic survey that has studied the prevalence of sexting and pornography use for the first time.
The decline in youth sexual activity is part of a wider trend of British people having less sex compared to previous generations, all revealed in the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), a survey of nearly 7,000 Britons between 2022 and 2024, which was published Tuesday in The Lancet medical journal.
Adults aged 45 and below are having sex twice a month on average, down from four times a month in 1990-91, and three in 2010-12, according to the survey. The proportion of 16- to 24-year-olds who said they had never had sex rose from 18% to 38% among women and 18% to 28% among men, compared to the previous Natsal study.
The latest survey was the first time participants had been asked about their online activity.
Half of the women respondents between 16 and 24 said they had watched pornography   in the past year, while 86% of young men said they had. Half of 16- to 24-year-olds said they had sent or received sexual images on their phone in the past year.
"There has been an emerging shift towards less sexual experience among young people," wrote the authors of the study. "Sexual lifestyles now commonly incorporate online behaviors such as sexting and pornography, especially for young people."
One of the researchers on the project, Prof. Wendy Macdowall at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, told CBS News partner BBC News that while it may be tempting to link the online activity with the decline in sexual activity, there are several other reasons for the drop, "especially among young people."
Similar declines among young people have been observed "in other high-income countries," the study states, and while "these changes are not yet well understood," it added, the shifts have coincided with rising rates of mental health conditions and declines in alcohol consumption, and "later attainment of traditional markers of adulthood," as well as "increasingly online lives."
Respondents reported an increase in masturbation across all age groups and genders, as well as sexting and pornography use, according to the survey's authors, but while that "might signal a shift away from partnered physical intimacy, towards more solo and online sexual behavior … masturbation and pornography use were lower among those reporting never having had sex, challenging the notion these behaviors simply substitute one another."
The study did not ask participants about any use of artificial intelligence in sexuality.
"When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi," Soazig Clifton, a researcher on the Natsal project from University College London, told the BBC. "In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behavior and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."
The study also revealed that the average number of sexual partners over a lifetime for people in the U.K. is five, and that same-sex intercourse has increased among both men and women.

articles.title_orig: A rising star in China is the latest victim of Xi’s purge
articles.title_zh: A rising star in China is the latest victim of Xi’s purge
articles.content_orig:
The Communist Party chief of Shanghai, considered a protege of Chinese leader Xi Jinping, has suddenly been placed under investigation –– marking an escalation of an anti-corruption purge that’s already ensnared a large swath of the country’s top talent .
Chen Jining, 62, who has run China’s largest city and financial center since October 2022, is facing a corruption charge and is suspected of “serious violations of discipline,” state media Xinhua said on Tuesday evening.
It is a stunning downfall for Chen, who was seen as a rising political star and even being mentioned among potential heirs to longtime leader Xi by China watchers.
Xi, who is all but certain to assume a precedent-breaking fourth term in office next year, has executed an unrelenting anti-corruption drive for well over a decade that has brought down senior political, military and judicial figures once thought untouchable. The speed and scale of that effort has reached unseen levels in recent months.
Chen becomes the fourth person from the 24-member politburo –– the top echelon of power in China –– to fall since the last party congress in 2022.
The investigation is being conducted by China’s main anti-corruption body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI).
Chen’s last public appearance seems to have been on Thursday, November 19, when he inspected the headquarters of a Chinese shipping conglomerate.
Unsurprisingly, government platforms in Shanghai have quickly taken down posts mentioning Chen.
China’s iron fist: Xi Jinping and the stakes for America
Trained as an environmental scientist, the urbane and English-speaking Chen rose through the party ranks in the past two decades. Before moving to Shanghai, he was mayor of Beijing and orchestrated the 2022 Winter Olympics in the capital.
His appointment to the top party job in Shanghai marked a quick elevation. The post usually paves the way for further promotion to the Politburo Standing Committee – the pinnacle of the party’s power structure. Both Xi and China’s former leader Jiang Zemin have followed this path.
It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
Prior to his Beijing mayoralty, Chen spent over a decade at the Ministry of Environment and Ecology. He also served as the president of Tsinghua University in Beijing, one of China’s most prestigious academic institutions.
After earning a master’s degree in civil and environmental engineering from Tsinghua in the 1980s, Chen went on to study at London’s Imperial College, where he earned a doctorate.
Just in the past two months, Xi’s clampdown on top officials brought the downfall of Beijing’s deputy mayor and a retired former mayor of Chongqing who had withstood several prior political storms.
The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission, is now down to only two members with one of those being Xi himself .
Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago, millions of rank-and-file officials have also been caught in his dragnet.
Between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials were convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption, according to official data from the CCDI – with more than 410 officials purged in the last three years alone.
