articles.title_orig: Chicago-bound American Airlines flight diverted to Phoenix; Video shows man being restrained
articles.title_zh: Chicago-bound American Airlines flight diverted to Phoenix; Video shows man being restrained
articles.content_orig:
CHICAGO -- A Chicago-bound American Airlines flight was forced to make an emergency landing after there was an apparent altercation on board.
American Airlines flight 1494 was headed from San Diego when it was diverted to Phoenix.
Video shows a man struggling with flight attendants.
A passenger who witnessed the incident said others on board jumped into action to help.
"It was remarkable how quickly everyone sprang into action to restrain this man and the flight attendants were remarkably orderly and calm," passenger Sean Bennett said.
Bennett said the plane landed safely and no one on board was hurt.
The FAA said in a statement, "American Airlines Flight 1494 landed safely at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport around 1 a.m. local time on Wednesday, Nov. 25, after the crew reported a passenger disturbance on board. The flight departed San Diego International Airport and was headed to Chicago O'Hare International Airport. The FAA will investigate."
American Airlines said in a statement, "American Airlines flight 1494 diverted to Phoenix (PHX) due to a disruptive customer. Upon arrival, law enforcement met the aircraft and assisted with deplaning the customer before the flight continued to its destination. The safety and security of our customers and team members is our top priority. We thank our team members for their professionalism and our customers for their assistance and under standing."
The Phoenix Police Department said in a statement, "On November 25, 2026, at approximately 1:00 a.m., a flight traveling from San Diego to Chicago diverted to Phoenix due to a passenger-related disturbance. According to preliminary information, the passenger left his assigned seat and moved to the front of the aircraft, where he repeatedly refused crew instructions to return to his seat and attempted to manipulate an aircraft door. Crew members and passengers restrained the individual until the aircraft landed safely at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.
"No injuries were reported among passengers or crew members. The passenger sustained a minor injury and was transported to the hospital for evaluation. The incident occurred while the aircraft was flying near the Arizona-California border south of Needles, California. The FBI was notified and will review the officer's reports. The flight was subsequently delayed while the airline addressed operational concerns.
"The incident remains under investigation."

articles.content_orig:
China Southern Airlines said in a filing late Tuesday that its subsidiary Xiamen Airlines had agreed to purchase 50 Boeing 737-8 aircraft with a combined catalog price of approximately $7.4 billion.
The announcement comes after President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he expected China to purchase another 250 Boeing aircraft, following his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit last week.
"By the way, I sold 250 Boeings to China, and I think they're going to do another 250," Trump said.
In May, China approved an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft for Chinese airlines following Trump's visit to Beijing, marking the country's first commitment to purchase U.S.-made Boeing aircraft since 2017, according to the White House.
It was not immediately clear whether Xiamen Airlines' latest purchase was part of that commitment.
China Southern, which owns a 55% stake in Xiamen Airlines, said the actual purchase price would be lower than the combined list price because of discounts offered by Boeing. The company did not disclose the final purchase price, citing confidentiality provisions in the agreement.
The aircraft are scheduled to be delivered in batches between 2031 and 2034, with the purchase financed through a combination of internal funds and external financing, the filing showed. The transaction remains subject to shareholder and relevant Chinese government approvals.
China Southern said the purchase would support Xiamen Airlines' planned relocation to the new Xiamen Xiang'an International Airport and the expansion of its route network.
The agreement follows the group's recent purchase agreement for 137 Airbus A320neo - family aircraft, the filing showed. China Southern said sourcing aircraft from different manufacturers would help diversify its fleet and improve operational flexibility.
Other Asian carriers, including Philippine Airlines and Malaysia Aviation Group , have also announced Boeing aircraft orders this month.

articles.title_orig: Bond market fears a Jensen flop more than Warsh going soft
articles.title_zh: Bond market fears a Jensen flop more than Warsh going soft
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent.
"We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China.
The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research.
Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack."
Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging.
More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models.
Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday.
"He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said.
"Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China.
Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention.
For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China.
As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added.
Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations.
In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive.
Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country.
It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore.
Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups.
She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options.
"There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI."
However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.
She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company.
The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S.
A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years.
"The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers.
Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high.
Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work.
It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu.
He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

articles.title_zh: Nvidia, AMD, and Micron stocks sink as investors flee AI trade
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock retreated another 8% on Wednesday, following a 6% decline in the prior session as chip stocks continued to plunge amid a broader market sell-off.
Peers AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) also extended losses from the prior session.
This year's once-hot AI trades continue to tumble, with memory chipmaker Micron Technology ( MU ) and peer SK Hynix ( SKHY ) tanking 11% and 8% respectively. Micron is more than 50% off its all-time high over the summer.
Storage and memory players Seagate (STX ), Western Digital ( WDC ), and Sandisk ( SNDK ) all fell on Wednesday. Sandisk, which recently implemented a stock split, is down roughly 70% from its June record high.
The violent move follows a stunning rally on Monday when Nvidia jumped 31% after the AI chip giant's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. But some strategists say tighter financial conditions and lingering questions around the AI trade are weighing on sentiment.
"There is still a lot of nervousness out there, and some investors have taken advantage of Monday's jump to cut their exposure to the AI trade," said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation, on Wednesday.
He also noted the prevailing view that Huang is the only person who can hold the AI trade together "reeks of desperation," while investors increasingly perceive that "Nvidia's board is not the one that the world's leading chip designer should want."
Other areas of the AI trade retreated on Wednesday, including the stocks of neocloud providers CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ), which each dropped by double-digit percentages.

articles.title_orig: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
articles.title_zh: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the U.S. Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.
The tariffs — rolled out early Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving — represent another controversial twist in Trump's economic policy. Voters in this month's midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump's policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll , a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.
Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year's tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.
The Trump administration argues that these countries have helped spur an influx of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies, creating a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.
The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. The official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes .
Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
The U.S. and China reached a trade truce last year that is set to expire on Jan. 10. The new tariffs will not come as a surprise to Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the administration official said.
Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China's purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.
The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted to specific products. They would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
Neither will they stack on top of levies of 10% to 12.5% announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The official said there are two other countries with pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.
The Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

articles.title_orig: Gold Holds Decline as US Tariff Plans Reinforce Rate-Hike Bets
articles.title_zh: Gold Holds Decline as US Tariff Plans Reinforce Rate-Hike Bets
articles.content_orig:
Kitco NEWS has a diverse team of journalists reporting on the economy, stock markets, commodities, cryptocurrencies, mining and metals with accuracy and objectivity. Our goal is to help people make informed market decisions through in-depth reporting, daily market roundups, interviews with prominent industry figures, comprehensive coverage (often exclusive) of important industry events and analyses of market-affecting developments.
(Kitco News) - The gold market continues to struggle to attract consistent bullish momentum as expectations that the Federal Reserve will maintain its hawkish monetary policies into the new year have driven real yields and the U.S. dollar higher, increasing the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.
However, Iggy Ioppe, Chief Investment Officer of Theo Network, a financial and tokenization platform, said that while gold has room to move lower in the near term, investors shouldn’t ignore the long-term, real-world value of holding the precious metal.
He added that while most investors are familiar with the old commodity market cliché that “the cure for high commodity prices is high prices,” the opposite is also true, especially when it comes to gold.
“The cure for low gold prices is low gold prices,” he said in an interview with Kitco News.
Ioppe explained that he divides the gold market into two distinct groups: momentum-driven investors, who amplify price movements, and self-correcting buyers, who become increasingly active as prices fall.
Although momentum-driven investors currently dominate the market, Ioppe said that lower prices should eventually stimulate physical demand from central banks, jewelry consumers and retail investors.
He noted that some central banks operate with fixed budgets for their gold purchases, meaning they can accumulate more of the precious metal as prices fall. At the same time, lower prices should help revive jewelry demand in China and India, where consumers are particularly price-sensitive.
“The self-correcting buyers, that’s medium and long term. A lot of the amplifying momentum buyers, they’re clustered in the very short term,” he said.
Ioppe added that there could also be significant pent-up investment demand from investors who sat on the sidelines during gold’s historic rally. He noted that many of the Wall Street and Silicon Valley investors he speaks with still have no exposure to the precious metal.
Unlike equities, where a significant decline in share prices could reflect a fundamentally broken business model, Ioppe said that gold’s underlying value proposition remains intact despite its recent selloff.
“ Gold is going to, at the minimum, keep up with the purchasing power,” he said.
Although Ioppe is not ruling out further selling pressure in the gold market, he questioned how sustainable the current environment of elevated real yields is, given the U.S. government’s deteriorating fiscal position.
He noted that yields on 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities have risen to roughly 2.9%, up from 1.8% a year ago. According to his analysis, roughly two-thirds of that increase reflects expectations of tighter U.S. monetary policy, while the remaining third reflects growing concerns about the creditworthiness of the U.S. government.
While higher real yields make Treasuries more attractive than gold in the near term, Ioppe said that investors will eventually have to recognize that some of those higher returns are compensation for taking on additional sovereign debt risk.
“It kind of creates the illusion of yield in the near term,” he said. “But at some point, people realize that there is no yield if there is risk embedded in it.”
Ioppe also warned that bond markets could be overly optimistic about the Federal Reserve’s ability to bring inflation back down to its 2% target.
He explained that the central bank’s ability to withstand political pressure has strengthened its credibility with financial markets. However, growing global economic fragmentation and trade barriers remain significant structural inflationary forces.
Looking ahead, Ioppe said that weaker employment data, softer inflation readings or a more dovish Federal Reserve could provide the catalyst gold needs to reverse its current momentum.
He added that lower oil prices could also provide some relief for the precious metal. Along with easing inflation pressures, lower energy prices would leave major gold-consuming nations, particularly those dependent on energy imports, with more capital to purchase gold.
Ioppe said that a recovery in investment demand could be particularly powerful as momentum-driven investors are forced to cover their short positions while physical buyers continue to take advantage of lower prices.
Beyond gold’s traditional fundamental drivers, Ioppe sees significant long-term potential in the growing tokenization of the precious metal, particularly as the technology addresses one of gold’s biggest shortcomings as an investment asset: its lack of yield.
Theo Network has developed gold and silver products that generate returns by leasing physical precious metals to industry participants, including refiners.
Ioppe explained that jewelers, bullion dealers and other industry participants could benefit from borrowing directly in gold rather than borrowing U.S. dollars to finance their inventories.( Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)
Although this financing model does not necessarily increase industrial demand for gold, he said that it could generate incremental investment demand by allowing a greater portion of the world’s above-ground gold stocks to generate a return.
“If they borrow from people that have physical gold, like us, and pay the interest in gold, that means a bigger percentage of the gold out there actually starts to pay yield, and that’s what creates incremental demand for gold,” he said.
While the tokenized gold market remains relatively small compared with the broader precious metals market, Ioppe said that its growing utility gives it a significant long-term advantage over traditional gold-backed exchange-traded funds.
Although ETFs have made gold more accessible to investors, he said that tokenization takes the precious metal beyond its role as a passive investment, allowing it to function more effectively as a monetary asset.
Even without generating a yield, tokenized gold can facilitate payments and wealth transfers, allowing consumers to hold their savings in gold rather than fiat currencies.
“ETF is a start. It’s good for investment, which is only one aspect of it,” he said. “Tokenized gold has utility. You can send it, you can pay for things, you can send tiny amounts. It’s available 24/7.”

articles.title_orig: China’s Huawei Convicted in U.S. Over Bank Fraud, Iran Ties
articles.title_zh: China’s Huawei Convicted in U.S. Over Bank Fraud, Iran Ties
articles.content_orig:
China’s biggest technology firm and the world’s largest telecommunications equipment maker has been convicted in the U.S. of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran.
Huawei was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts by a jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday. The verdict all but brings to a close an almost eight-year-long criminal case against Huawei and three of its subsidiaries. The sprawling legal case spanned a 12-week trial, dozens of witnesses, and hundreds of motions and filings.
It’s a rare case of U.S. prosecutors securing a conviction against a foreign corporation and could have significant consequences for both Huawei and U.S.-China relations.
The Justice Department first announced charges against Huawei in January 2019 as part of the first-term Trump Administration’s “China Initiative,” a controversial program to investigate and prosecute Chinese influence and espionage in the U.S.
The Shenzhen-based tech giant was found guilty of bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of U.S. sanctions. It faces massive potential penalties, including fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing is set for September 2027, with motions in advance of sentencing expected to start in the third week of January.
“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said .
James Barnacle Jr., assistant director in charge of the FBI’s New York office, added, “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”
The jury, however, acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: racketeering conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act (RICO).
Huawei’s attorney Brian Heberlig argued that U.S. prosecutors “began with guilt and worked backwards,” basing their claims of conspiracy on isolated incidents.
Huawei’s success, he said, is “about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig told reporters that the company will appeal the case.
“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” Huawei said in a statement . “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig speaks to reporters outside federal court in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Nov. 24, 2026. Larry Neumeister—AP
Huawei was convicted of conspiracy to steal trade secrets from U.S. companies over two decades. Its alleged theft includes router source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile, antenna technology from Quintel, and networking equipment information from Fujitsu Network Communications. The jury also found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and money laundering.
During the trial, which began Sept. 8, the jury watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei engineer unbolting and detaching the arm of a high-speed T-Mobile testing robot and slipping it into his backpack. The engineer said he found the piece in his bag, calling the incident a “mistake,” and returned it the next day after T-Mobile reported it missing, but not before a visiting engineer from China allegedly measured and photographed the robotic arm, according to prosecutors. Huawei later fired the employee.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei had hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by CNEX.
“Huawei cultivated a culture of crime and corruption, and that crime was an important business strategy,” U.S. prosecutor Taylor Stout said in his opening statement.
Huawei’s attorneys called 15 witnesses to give evidence that the company’s success came from its own innovation. The attorneys cited the company’s 110,000-person research and development team and its over 165,000 patents. Heberlig said prosecutors had “cherry-picked” instances of employee misconduct that were not representative of Huawei’s company culture.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei deliberately deceived global banks, including HSBC, BNP Paribas, and Standard Chartered, about its business in Iran and North Korea, which are both subject to U.S. sanctions. Huawei allegedly presented its Iran subsidiary, Skycom Tech, as an independent entity to skirt sanctions.
The jury, however, rejected the government’s assertion that Huawei had conspired in a racketeering scheme to expand its global business. If the company had been convicted of the RICO charge, it could have faced potential forfeiture of parts of its enterprise.
“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig, Huawei’s attorney, told reporters. The RICO charge, he said, “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
The jury also acquitted the company of conspiring to obstruct a federal grand jury investigation.
The legal case is among the most extensive against a corporation, involving millions of documents in evidence, covering source code, financial records, and emails. Jurors spent five days, beginning Nov. 18, deliberating the case.
“Rarely has a jury had to commit so much of their personal time to a trial,” U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly, who oversaw the case, said.
The case also took a winding path before the trial even began. It was delayed for years during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2022, U.S. prosecutors also charged two Chinese intelligence officers with trying to bribe a U.S. government employee with $61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and information about the case.
The case could have ramifications on the U.S.’s relationship with China. The verdict comes days after President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. It also comes amid tensions over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has renewed calls by U.S. lawmakers for tighter restrictions on A.I. chip sales to China .
Huawei, which is privately held, is one of China’s largest and most famous companies. The company reported 880.9 billion RMB ($126 billion) in revenue last year. It employs more than 200,000 employees globally and operates in more than 170 countries.
The case spawned a diplomatic crisis in 2018, when Canadian authorities detained Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou, who is also the daughter of the company’s founder, at the U.S.’s request. Meng had been secretly indicted on U.S. charges of bank and wire fraud.
Meng pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and fought extradition to the U.S. while under house arrest in Vancouver for nearly three years. She entered a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021, which acknowledged that she had misled an HSBC banker about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, after which she returned to China. A federal judge dismissed the charges against her with prejudice in December 2022. The HSBC executive Meng had met with in 2013 testified in the Brooklyn trial.
The first charges were announced as Washington and Beijing were locked in a trade war.
Since the first-term Trump Administration launched the “China Initiative” in 2018, federal prosecutors have secured convictions against a number of foreign nationals, but corporate cases have had mixed outcomes. Taiwan’s United Microelectronics pleaded guilty to stealing trade secrets in 2020, and China’s Hytera Communications pleaded guilty to conspiring to steal trade secrets in 2025. Chinese chipmaker Fujian Jinhua was acquitted in 2024. A separate federal case in Seattle against two Huawei subsidiaries has been repeatedly delayed, with a trial date set for October

articles.title_orig: China, US Hold First Agricultural Working Group Meeting
articles.title_zh: China, US Hold First Agricultural Working Group Meeting
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — President Trump has begun an extraordinary visit to Shenzhen, where he is set to join the leaders of Russia and China — two of Washington’s principal geopolitical rivals — for an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday.
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed Trump on the tarmac upon his arrival, reciprocating a rare honor Trump extended to him during his September visit to Washington.
All three leaders attended a dinner alongside other regional heads of government on Wednesday night, participating in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.
The trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind by leaders of the United States, Russia and China, three nations with the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
But while Trump has embraced a strategy of diplomatic engagement with historic foes, the three leaders enter the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Russian President Vladimir Putin hopes to secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine. Trump says he would like to discuss a nuclear arms control agreement and his war in Iran. And Xi aims to present China as a superpower on the international stage, capable of forging world peace.
Meeting with Putin before Trump arrived, Xi said that China’s relationship with Russia had remained as steadfast “as a rock through wind and rain.”
The two sides, he said, would pursue a “multipolar world” — a vision for a global balance of power that would see American influence weakened across Europe and Asia.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit.
Trump, for his part, has hedged on his expectations of the summit, signaling resolve against China ahead of his arrival here.
On Monday, the Trump administration tightened export controls on semiconductor chips essential to artificial intelligence development, closing loopholes aimed at curbing Chinese efforts to circumvent restrictions — a move that Trump acknowledged might be an “insult” to Xi before the meeting.
Chinese officials said Wednesday afternoon that Beijing reserved the right to retaliate.
“In essence, the United States is simultaneously trying to find limited avenues of cooperation with China while trying to clamp down on their access to critical parts of the AI supply chain, which doesn’t set up the conditions for productive dialogue,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump also met in Manila on Tuesday with fellow members of the Quad — India, Japan and Australia — in a show of resolve toward Beijing.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in the Philippines.
“We continue to protect peace through strength,” he added.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made a triumphant return to the semiconductor giant in an all-hands meeting Tuesday morning, apologizing to staff for his conduct during his previous stint at the company’s helm and vowing to do better this time around.
No company has impacted the world as deeply or profoundly as Nvidia, Huang said, according to an Nvidia employee who attended the meeting. Huang called the company’s story the most interesting in the world.
According to the individual, Huang expressed contrition for his past behavior and was adamant that employees should follow the company’s code of conduct. The AI hardware leader resigned from the company on Nov. 12 amid mounting scrutiny about alleged romantic relationships with subordinates and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence officials, Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
He also said that he has been regularly attending therapy and that he had been deeply embarrassed about recent events, the source said. The CEO was met with an overwhelmingly positive reception, even receiving a standing ovation, according to the source.
Huang’s return marked a nearly unprecedented case of corporate whiplash. After a wave of reports emerged stating that Huang had been involved in extramarital relationships — potentially with someone accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset — Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a letter sent to Nvidia employees and shared online on Nov. 8.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Huang wrote at the time. “I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”
Huang issued a personal statement on Nov. 17, expressing remorse but professing his admiration for and dedication to Nvidia. Huang founded the semiconductor designer in 1993 and grew it into what was once the world’s most valuable company.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang wrote in that statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Less than a week later, Nvidia’s board announced that Huang would return to the company — backed by “input from senior levels of the United States government” that essentially guaranteed “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Huang said in Tuesday’s meeting that President Donald Trump supported the company. “President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said, according to the Nvidia employee.
Huang said that Nvidia was an apolitical company. Huang added that he returned as CEO because the board — and not the government — had wanted him to be reinstalled.
The meeting, which kicked off around 9:30 a.m., lasted around an hour, according to the source, who added that Huang exited to the Foo Fighters’ song “Times Like These.”
Jean Lee reports with NBC News’ Social Newsgathering team in Los Angeles. She previously reported for the NBC News investigative unit.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.

US stock futures fell on Wednesday as investors braced for Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) data and monitored tech volatility ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
Futures on the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( YM=F ) declined by 0.3%, while those on the S&P 500 ( ES=F ) slid by 0.9%. Contracts for the Nasdaq-100 ( NQ=F ) fell 1%.
Markets started the day on a weaker footing after a sell-off in semiconductor stocks, with Nvidia ( NVDA ) shares losing nearly 6% Tuesday and continuing to decline on Wednesday. Despite Friday's major rally on Jensen Huang's Nvidia reinstatement, the AI trade has remained under pressure as questions about AI's profitability hammer stocks.
The focus on Wednesday turns to the latest PCE data and whether it shifts bets on the Federal Reserve's expected December rate hike. Core PCE, which excludes fuel and food and is the Fed's preferred inflation measure, is expected to tick up to 3.2% year over year. Traders are pricing in a 98% chance of a 25 basis point hike next month as they pull back odds of a 50 basis point hike.
The earnings calendar is light for the remainder of the week, with Deere ( DE ) reporting results today.
The stock and bond markets will be closed tomorrow in observance of Thanksgiving and will reopen Friday for a half-day of trading.

articles.title_orig: North Korea declares a Swiss diplomat persona non grata and orders him to leave
articles.title_zh: North Korea declares a Swiss diplomat persona non grata and orders him to leave
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has threatened to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month
SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea threatened Tuesday to close a Swiss diplomatic office that opened in Pyongyang last month, condemning Switzerland for imposing sanctions on a youth camp in eastern North Korea over its alleged role in the transfer of children from Russia-occupied areas of Ukraine .
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, described the Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan as an “open hostile act” and a “serious infringement” of the North’s sovereignty, according to a statement carried by state media.
Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials, said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia. She didn't directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be reeducated.
North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for economic assistance and military technology transfers.
Strengthened ties with Moscow and Beijing have been key drivers of Kim Jong Un’s increasingly assertive foreign policy as he positions North Korea as part of a united front against the United States.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to North Korea in late October as Switzerland opened a diplomatic office in Pyongyang and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation,” North Korean state media said at the time.
Kim Yo Jong said that North Korea would need to “comprehensively reconsider the relations with unreliable Switzerland” following the sanctions on the camp and called on North Korean diplomats to take unspecified “corresponding” countermeasures.
“It is my view that the Swiss diplomatic office has spontaneously lost justification for its existence, which was opened in Pyongyang under the pretext of improving the relations, given that the Swiss Confederation has clarified its stand not to respect the sovereignty of the DPRK,” she said, using the initials of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
In adding the Songdowon camp earlier this month to its broader sanctions related to Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine, Swiss authorities held the camp responsible for the “forced assimilation, including indoctrination, and militarized education of Ukrainian minors,” according to a document by Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs.
It said the camp participates in programs involving the transfer of Ukrainian children from Russia-occupied territories to North Korea and exposes them to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.
The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the Songdowon camp, freezing its assets and prohibiting financial transactions with the facility, although the practical impact of such measures is unclear given North Korea’s limited financial ties with European countries.
Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country, which has aggressively expanded its nuclear weapons program since Kim Jong Un took power in 2011.
The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in Pyongyang in 1997 that mostly focused on humanitarian programs, but the office closed in March 2020 as North Korea shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Swiss government has said that the new diplomatic office in Pyongyang, which reports to the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, would help strengthen direct contacts with North Korean officials and promote dialogue.
In a statement to The Associated Press, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said that it had taken note of North Korean statements. But it said that neither the Swiss Embassy in Beijing nor its diplomatic office in Pyongyang had been officially contacted about the matter. It said that Switzerland aims to “maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues.”
Kim Yo Jong's statement came a day after North Korean state media reported that Kim Jong Un received credentials from the newly appointed ambassadors from several countries, including Russia, Sweden, Indonesia, Vietnam, Brazil and India, in Pyongyang on Sunday.
During the ceremony, Kim Jong Un defended his efforts to strengthen his nuclear-armed military as necessary to protect the North’s security amid what he described as an “unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe,” Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency said.
Jamey Keaten contributed to this report from Geneva.

articles.title_orig: ‘Everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy’: Why Ukraine’s Med strike is a problem for Meloni
articles.title_zh: ‘Everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy’: Why Ukraine’s Med strike is a problem for Meloni
articles.content_orig:
Giorgia Meloni has a Ukraine problem.
With a national Italian election possible as early as this spring, Kyiv’s weekend strikes on a Russian warship and cargo vessel in Libya risk sparking a backlash in Rome — a Kyiv ally that also has traditionally close ties with the North African country.
“If this is a continuation of the war between Russia and Ukraine just a few hundred kilometers from Italy, this is worrying, especially because we work for the stability of Libya,” said Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, who added that Rome had not been informed ahead of time about the attack.
The Italian foreign ministry said Tajani spoke with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday.
"The Minister reiterated to his Ukrainian counterpart how vital it is for Italy to continue working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading to the Mediterranean as well," the ministry said in a statement . For Italy, "it is essential to respect Libya’s sovereignty and to continue working towards the country’s stability, unity and sovereignty."
Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League, a pro-Kremlin junior partner in Meloni’s governing coalition, that opposes further military aid to Ukraine said that “it wouldn't make sense” if military support provided to Ukraine “ends up making wars and sinking ships around the world.”
Kyiv defended its right to strike Russian vessels — even those docked in Benghazi, thousands of kilometers away from the battlefield.
The issue threatens to become a headache for Meloni.
Rome is especially concerned about destabilizing Libya, a former Italian colony, fearing that if the politically fragile country collapses into disorder again, it could spark a migration wave across the Mediterranean.
Russia and its allies in Libya could use migration as a weapon against the country, said Arturo Varvelli, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.
“For Italy, Libya is the most important foreign policy dossier because everything that concerns Libya concerns Italy,” said Lia Quartapelle, a center-left Democratic Party lawmaker and vice chair of the Foreign and European Affairs Committee of Italy’s parliament.
Meloni's strong backing for Ukraine puts her at odds with part of her coalition, as well as with large parts of the political opposition.
This summer, former Italian Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte, leader of the populist 5Star Movement, a key opposition party, set off a political firestorm by questioning further military aid to Ukraine if the center-left wins the next election.
The far-right opposition National Future Party, led by former Gen. Roberto Vannacci, also opposes military aid to Ukraine.
The public is also skeptical. Italians are the least likely to support Ukraine among major Western European countries, with a YouGov survey earlier this year finding that only 32% of Italians care if it wins against Russia.
For Meloni, "it’s a difficult match to handle," said pollster Lorenzo Pregliasco. "We [Italians] are afraid to take sides; we tend to be wary of conflict and of any Italian involvement in any conflict whatsoever."
That national caution has made Italy a relatively small donor to Ukraine — giving far less than countries like Germany or Nordic nations. Italy has provided around €3 billion in military aid, boosted by a new €800 million package.
Although there is worry about blowback, military giving "is unlikely to be affected in a meaningful way by the Ukrainian attacks," said Alessandro Marrone, who leads the defense, security and space program at Rome’s Istituto Affari Internazionali.
And it's not just Italy that is worried about a widening war in the Mediterranean.
“Greece’s government is concerned that the war in Ukraine could open another front in the eastern Mediterranean and is planning to have discussions on the issue with like-minded partners in the near future,” a senior Greek government official said.
Despite the turmoil in Rome and Athens, Kyiv stands by its decision to attack Russian ships.
“Ukraine is defending itself against the armed aggression of the Russian Federation. Our actions constitute the exercise of the inherent right to self-defense," Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters on Tuesday.
"Ukraine has the full right to strike the aggressor’s legitimate military targets. These include Russian warships, cargo vessels transporting military equipment and resources, and tankers belonging to the shadow fleet that sustain Russia’s war machine," he said. "Ukraine is not dragging anyone into the war, nor is it exporting the conflict elsewhere."
There is another risk for Meloni: that Ukraine ends up showing the lack of an Italian strategy in Libya to deal with the Russian presence there, said Varvelli, the ECFR researcher. The Russian naval vessel was sunk in the eastern Libyan port of Benghazi, controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army is allied with Moscow.
"The Ukrainians are simply bringing to light the significant Russian presence in Libya, which consists of six bases and between 1,000 and 1,500 personnel," he said, warning that Italy is “purely reactive” to what is happening in the country.
Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv and Nektaria Stamouli contributed reporting from Athens.

articles.title_orig: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.title_zh: China's Huawei says US conviction 'without legal or factual merit'
articles.content_orig:
A United States jury has convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
However, jurors on Tuesday acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge is typically used in organised crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from US companies.
The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.
Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.
US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.
The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.
Experts have said the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.
The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.
Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.
Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that did not actually exist.
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.
“That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together,” and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict “repudiated the central government narrative in the case”.
It is unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and the United Kingdom.
The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.
Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.
She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.
The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.
Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.
During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.
Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.
Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.
The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.
Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.
He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.
Huawei has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

articles.title_orig: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.title_zh: U.S.-China tensions could rise in 2027, but China could keep growing its exports: Economist
articles.content_orig:
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

articles.title_orig: See all of Trump’s Nvidia stock trades since January
articles.title_zh: See all of Trump’s Nvidia stock trades since January
articles.content_orig:
SALT LAKE CITY — Utah Sen. John Curtis said he agreed with tech CEO Jensen Huang's initial decision to step down from Nvidia and appeared skeptical about Huang's sudden reinstatement this week.
Huang's surprise comeback as head of one of the world's most prominent chip manufacturers was met with bipartisan pushback. Huang initially left the company after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump took credit for Huang's return to Nvidia. But the move prompted skepticism from some in Washington, including Curtis.
"Nvidia's board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk," the Republican senator wrote on X. "I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"
He added that Huang's initial decision to leave Nvidia after news of the affair broke was the right call.
"Just 11 days after Nvidia announced his departure, the board brought him back while its own independent investigation was still underway," Curtis continued. "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed."
Meanwhile, Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, has been quiet on social media about Huang and the controversy surrounding his role at Nvidia. A spokesperson did not immediately respond Tuesday when asked if Lee had any comment on Huang's reinstatement at the tech company.
Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, a Republican who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, called for Congress to investigate the situation.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," he wrote on social media. "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that is a customer of Nvidia. The alleged spy Huang had an affair with is a former executive for the company.
During a company-wide meeting Tuesday, Huang apologized to employees for making "some terrible mistakes," according to the New York Times , but he challenged the notion that he was back only because Trump pushed for it.
The president's involvement in the issue has raised questions about Nvidia's independence at a time when many are worried about a race with China to develop artificial general intelligence.
"In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company," Peter Cohan, associate professor of management practice at Babson College in Massachusetts, told the Associated Press . "That's because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it."
Former Utah Sen. Mitt Romney also weighed in on the latest AI developments on Tuesday, referring to the reported sales of AI chips to China.
"Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they'd need to get ahead of us," Romney wrote on X. "Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse."
The U.S. Department of Commerce has approved selling more than 800,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies this year, including companies with ties to the Chinese military, the New York Times reported last week. On Sunday, before Huang was renamed CEO, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for answers about Nvidia's chip sales to China.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers," he told CBS' "Face the Nation."

articles.title_orig: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.title_zh: I Designed My Dream Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale. It's Ridiculous
articles.content_orig:
Ferrari’s new 296 Challenge Stradale is a badass, 670-horsepower, non-hybrid race car for the road. Want one? It’ll cost you around $307,000 before options.
But if you want to get a little fancier with your new Ferrari, the automaker’s online configurator has plenty of ways to customize the supercar. And some of them are pretty wild. I wasted 30 minutes of my day dialing in my perfect 296 CS.
Let’s start with the most important part: paint. Ferrari offers a whopping 35 colors, split into four categories: Standard, Historical, Classic, and Special. You could go with the classic Rosso Corsa or Giallo Modena, but I'm going with something a little different here: Giallo Ambra, aka fancy orange.
Once you pick your paint, Ferrari lets you choose from a handful of livery options, including upper- and lower-body graphics, wing decals, door numbers, and more. Normally, I'd say a livery is mandatory on a car like this. But the 296 Challenge Stradale looks so damn good in a single color that it really doesn't need one.
Ferrari also lets you turn just about anything into carbon fiber. Front splitter? Carbon fiber. Rear diffuser? Carbon fiber. Even the engine covers? That's right, carbon fiber.
If you really want to go crazy, you can replace all the glass with Lexan, a lightweight polycarbonate that's a little lighter than traditional glass. That should help shave off a few pounds. Ferrari will even let you ditch the Prancing Horse badges on the front fenders entirely or swap the metal logos for painted ones.
Ferrari offers six wheel designs for the 296 CS, ranging from light silver to darker gray and black. You can also customize the wheel bolts, center caps, and more. I'm going with Forged Diamond-Polished wheels and titanium wheel bolts.
Depending on how you plan to use your 296 (primarily on road or track), Ferrari offers both Bridgestone and Pirelli tires. There are even two Pirelli "Color Edition" options with yellow or gray accents. We'll pass on those.
Brake calipers are available in eight different colors, ranging from black and red to yellow and silver.
Most of the interior upgrades are pretty subtle. You can choose floor mats with or without logos, pick from 26 stitching colors (we went with Filo Spec Flash Orange to match the exterior), and customize the lower portion of the dashboard with 22 different colors.
Perhaps the most important choice, though, is the seats. Ferrari offers two options: Racing and "Best Weight," as the automaker calls it. The racing seats appear to be lighter and probably less comfortable, but Ferrari doesn't really divulge any specifics.
There are seven different Alcantara colors available, depending on which seats you choose. You can also customize the seatbelts with six different colors, add a central racing stripe, and choose from additional stitching options.
Like most Ferraris, the 296 CS doesn't have a dedicated center touchscreen. That said, Ferrari does offer an optional passenger display, which seems a little odd in a car like this. Maybe your nephew can watch Shrek while you lap COTA. The world is your oyster.
As you'd expect, Ferrari doesn't list prices for any of these options in its configurator. You'll have to contact your local dealer to find out how much any of them will set you back.
But getting into a new 296 Challenge Stradale will cost you at least $307,000 to start. And that's before you start checking boxes.

articles.title_orig: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Almost three-quarters of a million Russian soldiers have been killed since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, equating to roughly one death every four minutes, analysis based on leaked official data has revealed.
Russian opposition outlets Mediazona and Meduza reported on Monday that by the end of September, 490,000 Russian troops had been confirmed dead by Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat.
But accounting for time lags in reporting and including troops who have been reported as missing in action – and are most likely dead – Russian fatalities jump to more than 720,000 since the start of the war, according to the two outlets.
That is a staggering number that surpasses Russia’s death toll from the Soviet war in Afghanistan in the 1980s and both Chechen wars in the 1990s and early 2000s – and which the Kremlin has long tried to keep secret.
The Ukraine-Russia war is seeping out across Europe and there are two reasons it will get worse
Rosstat stopped publishing demographic data in 2025 to disguise the rising death toll from the war. Mediazona and Meduza, as well as other outlets, obtained the official data after two pro-Ukrainian hacker groups, Cyber ​​Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow, managed to breach Rosstat’s servers earlier this month.
CNN cannot independently verify the figures, but the leaked data on confirmed deaths alone corroborates earlier estimates by analysts and Western intelligence – which now appear to fall far short of the likely real death toll.
Mediazona and Meduza have long been keeping a tally of Russian losses, based mostly on inheritance documents, death notices and other publicly available documents.
But the leaked Rosstat data allowed the media outlets to go a step further, using the same methods and calculations normally employed by actuaries estimating risks and insurance premiums.
By analyzing discrepancies between reported death dates and death registration dates, and by comparing these to search notices published by relatives, the reporters were able to extrapolate the number of deaths that have occurred but have not yet been reported to be somewhere around 230,000.
Mediazona has kept a tally of troops identified as missing by their relatives from 2023. That database contains 160,000 individuals and almost all of them are likely dead. Mediazona said that based on its reporting, the rate of survival among those reported missing only around 10%.
The data shared by Silent Crow showed that the war was the fourth most common cause of death in Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion, after heart diseases; Covid; and stroke and other vascular conditions. It also confirms what has long been suspected – that the losses are not spread evenly across Russia, with poorer areas and ethnic minorities suffering significantly higher casualty rates.
In addition, an analysis by the NEST Centre, a think tank that also obtained the data, revealed the scale of Russia’s recruitment of foreign fighters. It identified 6,947 records of foreign nationals killed in Ukraine – the majority of them from the central Asian countries of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkmenistan.
Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
Like Russia, Ukraine doesn’t release official casualty data, although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has publicly acknowledged the scale of losses in combat. The most recent research by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in July that the country has endured between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties, including 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities.
Alexander Baunov, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said that the combined death toll suffered by Russia and Ukraine could exceed 1 million.
As the newly projected death toll underscores the human cost of Moscow’s war, fears are growing in Ukraine over a deteriorating security situation in the country’s eastern Donetsk region – an area mostly under Russian control – amid daily guided bomb and drone attacks .
All families with children still in Donetsk were on Tuesday ordered to evacuate.
Children and families in many communities in most of Ukrainian-controlled Donetsk - including the major cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk - were already under the evacuation order, but now the measure has been expanded to settlements further west. An estimated 64,500 civilians remain in the region as of November 2026, according to the Donetsk regional military administration.
“This is an extremely difficult but necessary decision. The Russians are shelling our cities and villages every day and bombarding the region with aerial bombs,” said the head of Donetsk’s regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin.
For months, Moscow’s forces have been inching towards Kramatorsk , one of Ukraine’s last strongholds in the north of Donetsk region. Tuesday’s mandatory evacuation order is a sign of Kyiv’s concern that an expansion of Russian attacks could further harm civilians and isolate communities, for example by blowing up bridges and supply routes.
CNN’s Clare Sebastian, Nathan Hodge, Kosta Gak and Lauren Kent contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Blanche Downplays Questions Over Nvidia as Investigators Examine Company’s Customers
articles.title_zh: Blanche Downplays Questions Over Nvidia as Investigators Examine Company’s Customers
articles.content_orig:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed,  a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".
